> त्रि । सधस्था । सिंधवः । त्रिः । कवीनां । उत । त्रिमाता । विदथेषु । सम्‌राट् ।  
> ऋत्यवरीः । योषणाः । तिस्रः । अप्याः । त्रिः । अ । दिवः । विदथे । पत्यमानाः ॥ ५ ॥

> *tri | sadhasthā | siṃdhavaḥ | triḥ | kavīnāṃ | uta | trimātā | vidatheṣu | samrāṭ |*  
> *ṛtyavarīḥ | yoṣaṇāḥ | tisraḥ | apyāḥ | triḥ | a | divaḥ | vidathe | patyamānāḥ ‖ 5 ‖*

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> प्रजापतिः स्वविज्ञानं सिंधूनां निवेदयति । हे सिंधव आपः सर्वसाक्षिण्यो
> यूयं । त्री षधस्था त्रयो लोकाः । ते च प्रत्येकं त्रिर्भवंति ! तथा त्रयो वा
> इमे त्रिवृतो लोका इति श्रुतिः । न द्याव इंद्रमोजसा नांतरिक्षाणि वज्रीणं न
> विव्यचंत भूमयः । ऋग्वे. ८-६-१५ । इति प्रत्येकं बहुवचनश्रवणात् । बहुवचनं
> च कपिंजलन्यायेन त्रित्वे पर्यवसितं । ते च लोकाः कवीनां देवानां निवासस्थानानि भवंति । उतापि च त्रिमाता त्रयाणाममीषां लोकानां निर्माता संवत्सरः
> सूर्यो वा विदथेषु यज्ञेषु सम्राट् यजनीयतया सम्यग्दीप्यमानो वर्तते।
> तथा ऋतावरीरुदकवत्योऽप्या नभस्या आप्तव्या ना तिस्रो योषणास्त्रि संख्याका इलासरस्वतीभारतीत्येवंरूपाः परस्परमिश्रणोपेता देवता विदथे यज्ञॆ दिवो दिवसस्य
> तिस्त्रिषु सवनेष्वा पत्यमाना आगच्छंत्यो भवंति ॥ सधस्था । पूर्वपदादिति संहितायां
> षत्वं । योषणाः । युष इति सौत्रो धातुः । ल्युटि रूपं । लित्स्वरः । तिस्रः ।
> तिसृभ्यो जस इत्याद्यु दात्तत्वं । अप्याः । अप् इत्यंतरिक्षनाम । तत्र भवाः । भवे
> छंदसीति यत् । यतोऽनाव इत्याद्यु दात्तत्वं ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

Prajāpati declares his own knowledge to the rivers. "O rivers, waters, witnesses of all, you are त्री षधस्था (*trī ṣadhasthā*), the three worlds; and each of them is threefold." The Śruti says, "These three worlds are threefold." This is because the plural is heard for each of them, as in "न द्याव इंद्रमोजसा नांतरिक्षाणि वज्रीणं न विव्यचंत भूमयः (*na dyāva iṃdramojasā nāṃtarikṣāṇi vajrīṇaṃ na vivyacaṃta bhūmayaḥ*)" (Ṛg. 8-6-15); and the plural, by the kapiñjala rule, ends in the number three. Those worlds are the dwelling-places of the कवीनां (*kavīnāṃ*), the gods. Further, त्रिमाता (*trimātā*), the maker of these three worlds, the year or the sun, shines forth at the sacrifices (विदथेषु (*vidatheṣu*)) as सम्राट् (*samrāṭ*), fully resplendent as the one to be worshipped. Likewise the ऋतावरीः (*ṛtāvarīḥ*), those possessing water, the अप्याः (*apyāḥ*) ... नभस्या आप्तव्या ना (*nabhasyā āptavyā nā*)**NOTE**, the three women, three in number, of the forms Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, deities endowed with mutual mixing, come at the sacrifice during the three pressings of the day (दिवो दिवसस्य तिस्त्रिषु सवनेष्वा (*divo divasasya tistriṣu savaneṣvā*)).

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- सिंधवः (*siṃdhavaḥ*)—O waters in the form of streams
- कवीनां (*kavīnāṃ*)—for the gods
- त्रि षधस्था (*tri ṣadhasthā*)—the three worlds, which are dwelling-places
- त्रिः (*triḥ*)—are also of three forms
- उत (*uta*)—and
- त्रिमाता (*trimātā*)—the year (or the sun), who knows the measure of these three worlds**NOTE**
- विदथेषु (*vidatheṣu*)—at the sacrifices
- सम्राट् (*samrāṭ*)—has adorned the position of sovereign
- ऋतावरीः (*ṛtāvarīḥ*)—those filled with water

### Printed p. 356
- अप्याः (*apyāḥ*)—having the form of rain
- तिस्रः योषणाः (*tisraḥ yoṣaṇāḥ*)—the three women also
- विदथे (*vidathe*)—at the sacrifice
- दिवः त्रिः (*divaḥ triḥ*)—at the three pressing-times of the day
- आ पत्यमानाः (*ā patyamānāḥ*)—come down

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O waters in the form of streams, the three worlds, the dwelling-places of the gods, are also of three forms. And the year, or the sun, who knows the measure of these three worlds, has adorned the position of sovereign at the sacrifices. The three women, filled with water and having the form of rain, also come down every day at the three pressing-times of the sacrifice.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Rivers, the dwelling-places of the intelligent gods are thrice three; the measurer of the three (worlds) is the sovereign at sacrifices : three female (divinities) of the waters charged with the rains descend from heaven at the thrice (repeated) solemnity.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

A very profound meaning lies in this mantra. Seen superficially, three different ideas seem to illumine three separate points: first, the all-pervading lordship of the gods; second, the greatness of the year; third, the coming of the women at the three pressing-times. But on closer view these ideas are connected with one another and finally end in the exposition of a single principle.

Before understanding what it means that the three worlds are dwelling-places for the gods and that these three worlds are threefold (trivṛt), that is, have three forms, one must note what is distinctive in the use of the word कवि (*kavi*) as a synonym for the word देव (*deva*).

कवीनां (*kavīnāṃ*)—If कवीनां (*kavīnāṃ*) is taken to mean देवानां (*devānāṃ*), one and the same entity must be indicated by both words. The context must be one in which both words denote the same form and nature. One must therefore examine what the word देवानां (*devānāṃ*) indicates. When the etymologies of the names of gods such as Indra and Agni are given, the nature of the gods is also stated.

स योऽयं मध्ये प्राणः । एष एवेंद्रस्तानेष प्राणान्मध्यत इंद्रियेणैंद यदैन्थ तस्मादिंद इंधो ह वै तमिंद्र इत्याचक्षते परोक्षं परोक्षकामा हि देवास्त्रइद्धाः सत्त नाना पुरुषानसृजंत । (*sa yo 'yaṃ madhye prāṇaḥ | eṣa eveṃdrastāneṣa prāṇānmadhyata iṃdriyeṇaiṃda yadaintha tasmādiṃda iṃdho ha vai tamiṃdra ityācakṣate parokṣaṃ parokṣakāmā hi devāstraiddhāḥ satta nānā puruṣānasṛjaṃta |*) (Śa. Brā. 6-1-1-2)

### Printed p. 357
Among the vital airs within the body, the chief breath is well known as Indra. This chief breath kindles the other vital airs by its own power. Because it makes them blaze in this way, the name Indra became famous from this very quality of kindling (इंधानः (*iṃdhānaḥ*)). But one could simply call it इंधानः (*iṃdhānaḥ*); why then was it called Indra? Because the gods are always fond of what lies beyond the world. इंधानः (*iṃdhānaḥ*) would be a description in the manner of worldly poetry. To go beyond such worldly description and cross into the realm of the hidden is the mark of the gods. Hence the gods became famous as "lovers of the hidden".

अथ यो गर्भोऽंतरासीत् । सोऽग्रिरसृज्यत स यदस्य सर्वस्याग्रमसृज्यत तस्मादग्रिरग्रिर्ह वै तमग्निरित्याचक्षते परोक्षं परोक्षकामा हि देवाः । (*atha yo garbho 'ṃtarāsīt | so 'grirasṛjyata sa yadasya sarvasyāgramasṛjyata tasmādagriragrirha vai tamagnirityācakṣate parokṣaṃ parokṣakāmā hi devāḥ |*)
(Śa. Brā. 6-1-1-11)

The supreme principle that arose from the embryo within Brahman became famous as Agri. Because it was produced first of all beings in the universe, it was called Agri. The gods, who delight in the hidden sense, called this very one Agni. By these explanations the nature of the gods is described: it is the gods' character to convey, or reveal, or deepen the hidden meaning. This quality is common to gods and poets. A hidden meaning that lies beyond the ordinary human view is possible only for the gods. If that godhood is present in a man, he is called a poet (kavi). He has a vision better and more divine than that of an ordinary man. Though he has obtained human birth, he is reckoned a god.

विज्ञानमात्मानंदात्मनो हैव सर्वे देवाः सा हैषैव देवानामद्धाविद्या स ह स न मनुष्यो य एवंविद्देवानाग्ं हैव स एकः ॥ (*vijñānamātmānaṃdātmano haiva sarve devāḥ sā haiṣaiva devānāmaddhāvidyā sa ha sa na manuṣyo ya evaṃviddevānāgṃ haiva sa ekaḥ ‖*)
(Śa. Brā. 10-3-5-13)

Vijñāna means special knowledge. It is full of bliss; true knowledge is the cause of this bliss. Such true knowledge is possible for the gods, not for man. If anyone among men is able to obtain this knowledge, he too is reckoned a god; thus the nature of godhood is shown. For this very reason they have explained the word kavi as "one who sees beyond" (krāntadarśin). The Nirukta authors have read this word among the names of the intelligent, कविः (*kaviḥ*), मनीषी (*manīṣī*) and so on (Ni. 3-15).

मेधावी कविः क्रांतदर्शनो भवति कवतेर्वा (*medhāvī kaviḥ krāṃtadarśano bhavati kavatervā*)
(Ni. 12-13)

### Printed p. 358
The Nirukta authors' derivation is that this word, formed from the root क्रम् (*kram*), means one whose vision goes beyond, or, formed from the root कम् (*kam*), means a worshipper who praises. Both derivations show an intellect and a disposition that grasp the true meaning. Just as the example above explains that the gods have the power to obtain knowledge of the highest truth, so the poet too has an unworldly and extraordinary power of knowing all affairs of past, present and future. On many occasions Sāyaṇa has said that देव (*deva*) is a synonym of the word kavi. Although he is a man, the poet has godhood in him because he has divine sight; and the sense is that he has a power beyond the human. Though physically he has two eyes, his inner eye equals a thousand eyes.

सहस्रणीथाः कवयो ये गोपायंति सूर्यं । यमहीन् तपस्वतो यम शपोजा अपि गच्छतात् ॥ (*sahasraṇīthāḥ kavayo ye gopāyaṃti sūryaṃ | yamahīn tapasvato yama śapojā api gacchatāt ‖*)
(Ma. Saṃ. 0-154-5) **NOTE**

The poets have a thousand eyes and see beyond; they have the power to protect even the Āditya. [A thousand-eyed one may mean one with a thousand eyes, or a guide to thousands of followers. If "guide" is meant, it means one who knows the meaning of the principle and has the power to teach others.] Because they have such power,

समुद्रे अंतः कवयो वि चक्षते मरीचीनां पदमिच्छंति वेधसः (*samudre aṃtaḥ kavayo vi cakṣate marīcīnāṃ padamicchaṃti vedhasaḥ*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-177-1)

these poets who see beyond know the supreme principle that dwells within the orb of the Āditya, and they also desire to attain identity with it. Moreover,

तां द्योतमानां स्वर्यं मनीषामृतस्य पदे कवयो नि पांति (*tāṃ dyotamānāṃ svaryaṃ manīṣāmṛtasya pade kavayo ni pāṃti*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-173-2)

ऋतस्य पदं कवयो नि पांति गुहा नामानि दधिरे पराणि (*ṛtasya padaṃ kavayo ni pāṃti guhā nāmāni dadhire parāṇi*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-5-2)

Thus the power of the poets is described: the poets, who see beyond and possess godhood, enter the path of Ṛta and know the most hidden and most exalted secret. (This same matter is explained in detail in the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā, Part 13, pp. 377-379.) Because this extraordinary power is also revealed in the present mantra, the synonym कवीनां (*kavīnāṃ*) is used to designate the gods. Such gods pervade the universe; therefore they are त्रिषधस्थ (*triṣadhastha*).

### Printed p. 359
त्रिषधस्था—त्रयो लोकाः देवानां निवासस्थानानि भवंति । (*triṣadhasthā—trayo lokāḥ devānāṃ nivāsasthānāni bhavaṃti |*) The three worlds are the dwelling places of the gods. Each of these is again of three kinds.

तिस्र एव देवता इति नैरुक्ताः । अग्निः पृथिवीस्थानः । वायुर्वा इंद्रो वा अंतरिक्षस्थानः । सूर्यो द्युस्थानः ॥ तासां महाभाग्यात् एकैकस्या अपि बहूनि नामधेयानि भवंति ॥ (*tisra eva devatā iti nairuktāḥ | agniḥ pṛthivīsthānaḥ | vāyurvā iṃdro vā aṃtarikṣasthānaḥ | sūryo dyusthānaḥ ‖ tāsāṃ mahābhāgyāt ekaikasyā api bahūni nāmadheyāni bhavaṃti ‖*)
(Ni. 7-5)

For the three deities Agni, Vāyu or Indra, and Āditya, the three worlds are the abode: the earth for Agni, the atmosphere for Vāyu or Indra, the heaven-world for Āditya. The Nirukta authors say that because of their greatness they have endless other names too, and thus describe the nature of the gods who occupy these three worlds. The Ṛk Saṃhitā likewise states that the three worlds are the abode of these three deities, who have endless varieties:

सूरो नो दिवस्सातु वातो अंतरिक्षात् । अग्निर्नः पार्थिवेभ्यः (*sūro no divassātu vāto aṃtarikṣāt | agnirnaḥ pārthivebhyaḥ*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-158-1)

When it is prayed that Sūra of the heaven-world, Vāyu of the atmosphere and Agni of the earth protect us, the three worlds indicated by त्रिषधस्था (*triṣadhasthā*) are described.

The word सधस्थ (*sadhastha*) means a common place. In some places this word is also a synonym for the atmosphere. It is also customary to call the altar-place where all the priests sit together and perform the sacrifice सधस्थ (*sadhastha*). Moreover, as has been said earlier, Sāyaṇa in his commentary on Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-154-1 explains it as सधस्थं सह स्थानं पुण्यकृतां सहनिवासयोग्यं भूरादिलोकसप्तकं । (*sadhasthaṃ saha sthānaṃ puṇyakṛtāṃ sahanivāsayogyaṃ bhūrādilokasaptakaṃ |*), the seven worlds where the virtuous may dwell, or सहस्थानं सत्यलोकं (*sahasthānaṃ satyalokaṃ*), the Satya world, which is above all worlds and is the highest of all. Looking at त्रिषधस्था (*triṣadhasthā*) in the present passage, it is not easy to state the precise meaning. The order earth, atmosphere, heaven-world for the three deities Agni, Vāyu and Sūra is probably stated in many places. But in the Śatapatha and other texts a special feature is shown in this context:

ब्रह्म वा इदमग्र आसीत् । तद्देवानसृजत । तद्देवान्त्सृष्टैषु लोकेषु व्यारोहयदस्मिन्नेव लोकेऽग्निं वायुमंतरिक्षे दिव्येव सूर्यं । अथ येऽत ऊर्ध्वा लोकाः । तद्या आत ऊर्ध्वा देवतास्तेषु ता देवता व्यारोहयत् (*brahma vā idamagra āsīt | taddevānasṛjata | taddevāntsṛṣṭaiṣu lokeṣu vyārohayadasminneva loke 'gniṃ vāyumaṃtarikṣe divyeva sūryaṃ | atha ye 'ta ūrdhvā lokāḥ | tadyā āta ūrdhvā devatāsteṣu tā devatā vyārohayat*)
(Śa. Brā. 11-2-3-1)

### Printed p. 360
Brahman, who existed before the creation of the universe, created the three deities beginning with Agni and established them in the three worlds beginning with the earth. But the deities more exalted than these he established in three worlds more exalted than the earth and the rest. This is what is said. Continuing the same matter, there is an explanation that shows the unity of all the worlds. Explaining what is meant by the three worlds being threefold (trivṛt), and what the purport is, Sāyaṇa says that in the Ṛk

न द्याव इंद्रमोजसा नांतरिक्षाणि वज्रिणं । न विव्यचंत भूमयः (*na dyāva iṃdramojasā nāṃtarikṣāṇi vajriṇaṃ | na vivyacaṃta bhūmayaḥ*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-6-15)

the plurals "heavens", "atmospheres", "earths" occur, and that it should be understood here in the same way. But how the threefold division is, he has not said. Later, in the commentary on the same Ṛk 8-6-15, he relies on the Āraṇyaka sentence cited, saying that they are threefold as stated in the sentence त्रयो वा इमे त्रिवृतो लोकाः (*trayo vā ime trivṛto lokāḥ*) (I. Ā. 1-1-2) **NOTE**. Here too the nature of the three divisions is not stated. Moreover, he says that it should be understood here as in the mantra

तिस्रो भूमीर्धारयन् त्रीग्ंरुत द्यून् त्रीणि व्रता विदथे अंतरेषां (*tisro bhūmīrdhārayan trīgṃruta dyūn trīṇi vratā vidathe aṃtareṣāṃ*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-27-8)

But in the cited 2-27-8 it does not mean that the earth itself is threefold. In this very Ṛk Sāyaṇa says आत्र भूमिशब्दः लोकत्रये वर्तते (*ātra bhūmiśabdaḥ lokatraye vartate*): here the word bhūmi means the three worlds. Hence it is understood that it does not mean the earth is of three kinds. He says it should be understood here as in the sentence "यो द्वितीयस्यां तृतीयस्यां पृथिव्यां (*yo dvitīyasyāṃ tṛtīyasyāṃ pṛthivyāṃ*)". Whether, therefore, the earth and the rest are each individually of three kinds, or whether naming one is as if naming the other three as well, will be examined later.

त्रिमाता—त्रयाणां अमीषां लोकानां निर्माता संवत्सरः सूरोऽन्या । (*trimātā—trayāṇāṃ amīṣāṃ lokānāṃ nirmātā saṃvatsaraḥ sūro 'nyā |*) The year, or Sūrya, the maker of these three worlds beginning with the earth. Since the description विदधेषु सम्राट् (*vidadheṣu samrāṭ*) is present, one must examine whether त्रिमाता (*trimātā*) means the year alone, or Sūrya alone, or whether being sovereign in the sacrifice (vidatha) is natural to both the year and Sūrya. How

### Printed p. 361
Sūrya can be the triple maker and sovereign in the sacrifice, so, only if the year also has both functions, is त्रिमाता (*trimātā*) here one of the two; that is the purport.

The year too has obtained the quality of triple maker only through Āditya. The relation of Āditya and the year is itself the root of the origin of all gods, men and the rest in the three worlds. Agni, Āditya and the year, these three principles are the lords of the sacrifice. From the union of these three the sacrifice arises; the sacrifice is the root of creation, and the sacrifice is the root of this union. Thus the identity of cause and effect also explains the beginninglessness of creation and the relation of sacrifice to creation.

अप्पु हिमे लोकाः प्रतिष्ठिता आदित्य आसज्जनमादित्ये हीमे लोका दिग्भिरासक्ताः....संवत्सर एषोऽग्निर्यतवः शिक्क्यमृतुभिर्हि संवत्सरः शक्नोति.... (*appu hime lokāḥ pratiṣṭhitā āditya āsajjanamāditye hīme lokā digbhirāsaktāḥ....saṃvatsara eṣo 'gniryatavaḥ śikkyamṛtubhirhi saṃvatsaraḥ śaknoti....*)
(Śa. Brā. 6-7-1-17, 18)

The principle of creation set out in such sentences, and its relation to the principle of sacrifice, will also be explained later in the commentary on the Puruṣa Sūkta.

विधथेषु (*vidhatheṣu*)—The use of the word vidatha in the senses of knowledge, sacrifice, sacrificial assembly, observance of rule, and the sacrificial power indicated thereby, has been explained earlier.

तिस्रः योषणाः आ पत्यमानाः (*tisraḥ yoṣaṇāḥ ā patyamānāḥ*) At the time of sacrifice three women descend. The commentator says they are Iḷā, Bhāratī and Sarasvatī. The nature of these three deities has been told earlier, when the Āprī Sūktas were explained (Ṛgveda Saṃhitā Part 11, pp. 263-266). Even so, in the present passage, where the description is headed by Āditya, one must examine what relation these three deities, who have a sacrificial connection, have with Āditya.

देव्यस्ति स्रः श्रिताश्चैनं त्वष्टा चैवैतदाश्रयः (*devyasti sraḥ śritāścainaṃ tvaṣṭā caivaitadāśrayaḥ*)
(Bṛ. De. 1-108)

A sentence of the Bṛhaddevatā says that the three goddesses have resorted to this Agni and are contained within Agni; and in the sentences that follow it is stated still more clearly:

तिप्रस्तु देव्यो याः प्रोक्तास्तिस्थानैवेह सा तु वाक् । त्रिविधेनोच्यते नाम्ना ज्योतिषु त्रिषु वर्तिनी ॥ अग्निमेवानुगेळा तु मध्यं प्राप्ता सरस्वती । अमू स्थिताधिलोकं तु भारती भवति ह्यसौ ॥ सैषा तु त्रिविधा वाग्वै दिवि च व्योम्नि चेह च । व्यस्ता चैव समस्ता च भजत्यग्नीनिमानपि ॥ (*tiprastu devyo yāḥ proktāstisthānaiveha sā tu vāk | trividhenocyate nāmnā jyotiṣu triṣu vartinī ‖ agnimevānugeḷā tu madhyaṃ prāptā sarasvatī | amū sthitādhilokaṃ tu bhāratī bhavati hyasau ‖ saiṣā tu trividhā vāgvai divi ca vyomni ceha ca | vyastā caiva samastā ca bhajatyagnīnimānapi ‖*)
(Bṛ. De. 3-12 to 14)

### Printed p. 362
अयं प्रयोगस्त्वेतेषां ज्योतिषां त्रिषु वर्ततां । (*ayaṃ prayogastveteṣāṃ jyotiṣāṃ triṣu vartatāṃ |*)
(Bṛ. De. 1.90)

त्रिसो देव्यति (*triso devyati*) means the presiding goddesses of speech, who are in the three worlds. Of them Iḷā followed the earthly Agni; Sarasvatī occupied the middle world; Bhāratī became resident in the heaven-world. Yet all three goddesses serve the earthly Agni. In some places the word इळा (*iḷā*) is explained as food in the form of the oblation. In इळायास्पुत्रो वयुनेऽजनिष्ट (*iḷāyāsputro vayune 'janiṣṭa*) the relation of Iḷā to Agni is shown. Epithets such as धृतपदी धृतहस्ता (*dhṛtapadī dhṛtahastā*) are likewise words indicating a connection with Agni.

आ नो यज्ञं भारती ताम्रमेवा मनुष्पदिह चेतॆयंती । तिस्रो देवीर्बर्हिरेदं स्योनं सरस्वती स्वपसः सदंतु ॥ (*ā no yajñaṃ bhāratī tāmramevā manuṣpadiha cetèyaṃtī | tisro devīrbarhiredaṃ syonaṃ sarasvatī svapasaḥ sadaṃtu ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-110-8)

Citing this Ṛk, the Nirukta authors have explained the above purport clearly. भरतः आदित्यः तस्य भाः भारती (*bharataḥ ādityaḥ tasya bhāḥ bhāratī*) (Ni. 8-13): Bharata is Sūrya; his radiance is named Bhāratī. सर इत्युदकनाम । तद्वती स्तनितादिरूपा माध्यमिका च वाक् । (*sara ityudakanāma | tadvatī stanitādirūpā mādhyamikā ca vāk |*): Sarasvatī is a transformed form of the atmospheric goddess of speech, who has water and the sound of thunder and the like. Thus Bhāratī is the radiance of Āditya of the heaven-world; Sarasvatī is the manifestation of Vāyu of the atmosphere; Iḷā is the radiance of the earthly Agni. In this way these three deities, as representatives of the three worlds, give primacy to the sacrifice and take part in it. Moreover,

तस्मा अग्निर्भारतः शर्म यंसज्योक्षश्यात्सूर्यमुच्चरंतं ॥ (*tasmā agnirbhārataḥ śarma yaṃsajyokṣaśyātsūryamuccaraṃtaṃ ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-25-4)

Since in this Ṛk the word भारतः (*bhārataḥ*) is an epithet of Agni, some hold that the radiance connected with him may be named Bhāratī.

होतायक्षत्तिस्रो देवीरपसामपस्तमा अच्छिद्रमद्येदमपस्तन्वतां । देवेभ्यो देवीर्देवमपो वियंत्वाज्यस्य होतरज ॥ (*hotāyakṣattisro devīrapasāmapastamā acchidramadyedamapastanvatāṃ | devebhyo devīrdevamapo viyaṃtvājyasya hotaraja ‖*)
(Śai. Brā. 3-6-2-2) **NOTE**

In explaining this sentence of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa it is said: इडा,सरस्वती, भारतीत्येवंरूपास्तिस्रोऽष्टमप्रयाजदेव्यस्तद्रूपमग्निं दैव्यो होता यजतु । (*iḍā,sarasvatī, bhāratītyevaṃrūpāstisro 'ṣṭamaprayājadevyastadrūpamagniṃ daivyo hotā yajatu |*). Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī, these three are the deities of the eighth prayāja mantra, goddesses that reflect Agni.

### Printed p. 363
This Agni, the lord of the whole sacrifice, who has all three of these forms, is the Āditya described in the present Ṛk.

एतद्भूतेषु लोकेषु अग्निभूतं स्थितं त्रिधा । ऋषयो गीर्भिरर्चंति व्यंजितं नामभिस्त्रिभिः ॥ (*etadbhūteṣu lokeṣu agnibhūtaṃ sthitaṃ tridhā | ṛṣayo gīrbhirarcaṃti vyaṃjitaṃ nāmabhistribhiḥ ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 1-64)

This Agni is present in all beings and in all worlds, and he abides in the form of fire. He became manifest in a different form in each of the three worlds, and he is praised under the names Agni, Vāyu and Āditya. The three powers who are special manifestations of such an Agni (Iḍā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī) are asked to come at the three times of pressing (savana) and see that the sacrifice is completed in all its parts.

#### Ṛk 6

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> त्रिरा दि॒वः स॑वित॒र्वार्या॑णि दि॒वेदि॑व॒ आ सु॑व॒ त्रिर्नो॒ अह्नः॑ ।  
> त्रि॒धातु॑ रा॒य आ सु॑वा॒ वसू॑नि॒ भग॑ त्रातर्थिषणे सा॒तये॑  
> धाः ॥ ६ ॥

> *trirā divaḥ savitarvāryāṇi divediva ā suva trirno ahnaḥ |*  
> *tridhātu rāya ā suvā vasūni bhaga trātarthiṣaṇe sātaye*  
> *dhāḥ ‖ 6 ‖*

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> त्रिः । आ । दिवः । सवितः । वार्याणि । दिवेऽदिवे । आ । सुव । त्रिः । नः । अह्नः ।  
> त्रिधातु । रायः । आ । सुव । वसूनि । भग । त्रातः । धिषणे । सातये । धाः ॥ ६ ॥

> *triḥ | ā | divaḥ | savitaḥ | vāryāṇi | dive 'dive | ā | suva | triḥ | naḥ | ahnaḥ |*  
> *tridhātu | rāyaḥ | ā | suva | vasūni | bhaga | trātaḥ | dhiṣaṇe | sātaye | dhāḥ ‖ 6 ‖*

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> सवितः सर्वस्य प्रेरक हे आदित्य दिवो द्युलोकादागत्य त्वं वार्याणि सर्वैः
> संभजनीयानि धनानि दिने दिने प्रतिदिनं त्रिरा सुव । त्रिवारमस्मभ्यं प्रेरय । प्रयच्छेत्यर्थः । तदेवोच्यते । भग सर्वैर्भजनीय त्रातरस्माकं रक्षक हे आदित्य त्रिधातु
> त्रिधातूनि पशुकनकरत्नभेदेन त्रिप्रकाराणि वसूनि धनानि रायः । रांति क्षीरादीनीति
> रायो गोधनानि । तानि च नोऽस्मभ्यमह्नः संबंधिषु त्रिस्त्रिषु सवनेष्वा सुव ।
> प्रयच्छ । धिषणे माध्यमिके हे वाक् सातये धनलाभाय धाः । आस्मान् कुरु ॥
> त्रिः । द्वित्रिचतुर्भ्यः सुच् । पा ५-४-१८ । इति सुच् । चित्स्वरः । सुव । शू प्रेरणे ।
> तुदादिः । लोटि रूपं । त्रिधातु । डुधाण् धारणपोषणयोरित्यस्मात्सितनिगमिमसीत्यादिना तुन्प्रत्ययः । धिषणे । आमंत्रितत्वान्निघातः ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

"Savitṛ" is the impeller of all. Sāyaṇa addresses him as Āditya: "O Āditya, coming from the heavenly world, bestow on us every day, three times, the desirable (vāryāṇi) riches that all may enjoy." Ā suva means "impel, give." He then says what is asked. "Bhaga" is the one whom all revere, and "trātṛ" is our protector, so both address Āditya. "Tridhātu" means riches (vasūni) of three kinds: cattle, gold and jewels. "Rāyaḥ" means cattle-wealth, so called because it gives (rānti) milk and so on. These riches are to be given to us at each of the three pressings belonging to the day. "Dhiṣaṇe" is the middle (mādhyamikā) Vāk; "sātaye" means for the gain of wealth, and "dhāḥ" means "make us (so)."

### Printed p. 364

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- सवितः (*savitaḥ*)—O Āditya, impeller of the world
- दिवः (*divaḥ*)—coming from the heavenly world
- वार्याणि (*vāryāṇi*)—riches desired by all
- दिवेदिवे (*divedive*)—every day
- त्रिः (*triḥ*)—at the three times
- आ सुव (*ā suva*)—supply
- भग (*bhaga*)—O Āditya, in the form of Bhaga, revered by all
- त्रातः (*trātaḥ*)—protector
- त्रिधातु (*tridhātu*)—in the forms of cattle, gold and jewels
- वसूनि (*vasūni*)—riches
- रायः (*rāyaḥ*)—wealth in the form of cattle
- नः (*naḥ*)—to us
- अह्नः (*ahnaḥ*)—of each day
- त्रिः (*triḥ*)—at the time of the three pressings
- आ सुव (*ā suva*)—supply
- धिषणे (*dhiṣaṇe*)—O middle Vāk
- सातये (*sātaye*)—for the gain of our wealth
- धाः (*dhāḥ*)—show favour

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

O Āditya, impeller of the world, come from the heavenly world and supply, every day at the three times, the riches that all desire. O Āditya, in the form of Bhaga, revered and protector of all, supply to us at the three pressings of each day riches in the form of cattle, gold and jewels, and wealth in the form of cattle. O goddess Vāk of the middle region, show favour so that we may gain wealth.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Savitri, desended fron heaven, bestow upon us blessings thrice every day: Bhaga, saviour, grant us thrice a day riches of three elements: Dhishana enable us to acquire (wealth).

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In this mantra a prayer for the wealth desired is addressed to three deities: Savitṛ, Bhaga and Dhiṣaṇā. The sense is that these three preside over the three kinds of wealth and bestow it. From Āditya the "tridhātu" is asked for.

The word "tridhātu" has been explained as wealth in the form of cattle, gold and jewels. The word is used in many places with different meanings. Where it is used for the principles (tattva) in the form of earth, water and fire, or for the qualities (guṇa) in the form of sattva, rajas and tamas, this has been explained in detail in Ṛgveda Saṃhitā Part 11, pp. 583-586.

"Dhiṣaṇe": this word is read among the names of heaven and earth, along with "svadhe" and "purandhī" (Ni. 3-21). धिषणा वाक् धिषेर्दधात्यर्थे धीसादिनीति वा (*dhiṣaṇā vāk dhiṣerdadhātyarthe dhīsādinīti vā*) (Ni. 8-3). It is said that the word may be derived from the root धिष् (*dhiṣ*), which gives the sense "holds." Or, "dhīsādinī iti vā": it extends the intellect, that is, it makes the meaning clear. This is

### Printed p. 365
the view of the Nirukta authors. In some places Sāyaṇa has explained it as Vāk in the form of mantra, and in others as the middle Vāk. In some places, such as मा च्येद्म रश्मी .... .... धिषणाया उपस्थे (*mā cyedma raśmī .... .... dhiṣaṇāyā upasthe*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-109-3), it means the bag that holds the Soma juice, as was explained earlier.

The word is used in all three numbers, and in some contexts its meaning has to be decided from the number and from the context.

When it is in the singular, it means Vāk, praise in the form of speech, or the bag that holds Soma juice. In places such as वैश्वानराय धिषणां (*vaiśvānarāya dhiṣaṇāṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-2-1) it can easily be said to mean praise.

When the dual "dhiṣaṇe" is used, it generally means heaven and earth. It is formed from the root धिष् (*dhiṣ*), meaning "hold firmly," and it is a synonym for heaven and earth, which hold all the worlds. प्रजापतिर्वै प्रजाः सृष्ट्वा ता द्यावापृथिवीभ्यां पर्यागृह्णात् (*prajāpatirvai prajāḥ sṛṣṭvā tā dyāvāpṛthivībhyāṃ paryāgṛhṇāt*) (Śa. Brā. 3-8-4-17). It may be said that heaven and earth keep under their control and bear all the worlds created by Prajāpati, and are therefore known as "dhiṣaṇe."

But where the plural is used in some places, it is not easy to state the meaning of the word.

इरावतीर्वरुण धेनवो वां मधुमद्वां सिंधवो मित्र दुह्रे । त्रयस्तस्फुर्वृषभासस्ति सृणाः धिषणानां रेतोधा वि द्युमंतः ॥ (*irāvatīrvaruṇa dhenavo vāṃ madhumadvāṃ siṃdhavo mitra duhre | trayastasphurvṛṣabhāsasti sṛṇāḥ dhiṣaṇānāṃ retodhā vi dyumaṃtaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-69-2)

Here heaven and earth, together with the atmosphere within them, are included, so Sāyaṇa has explained "dhiṣaṇānām" as "of earth, atmosphere and heaven." But in this place that meaning is not directly indicated by the word. He first explains "dhiṣaṇānām" as "sthānānām" (of the places), and then, asked what the places are, explains them as the three worlds. This meaning was given earlier in the explanation of the word "dhiṣṇya." Besides this, in some other places where the plural is used, even Sāyaṇa shows a little difficulty. For example:

The passage beginning धिषणास्ता देवीः (*dhiṣaṇāstā devīḥ*) (Śa. Brā. 6-5-4-5) **NOTE**

### Printed p. 366
These Dhiṣaṇās are dear to all the gods. They are made to blaze at the seat (sadhastha) of the earth. These Dhiṣaṇās, ancient, of divine form and dear to all the gods, are manifestations of the goddess Vāk. It is with the help of speech that everything is kindled and illumined. Where such a description is given, a hidden, essential meaning is present.

The word "dhiṣaṇe" is in the dual, and it can also be a vocative. In the present mantra, "he mādhyamike vāk" (O middle Vāk) addresses the goddess Vāk.

"Sātaye": it is formed from the root सन् (*san*), which gives the sense "obtain." Words such as वाजसातिः (*vājasātiḥ*) and वाजसातये (*vājasātaye*) are well known. Here the prayer is to show favour so that wealth may be obtained.

#### Ṛk 7

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> त्रिरा दि॒वः स॑वि॒ता सो॑षवीति॒ राजा॑ना मि॒त्रावरु॑णा सुपा॒णी ।  
> आप॑श्चि दस्य॒ रोद॑सी चिदु॒र्वी रत्नं॑ भिक्षंत सवि॒तुः स॒वाय॑॥ ७ ॥

> *trirā divaḥ savitā soṣavīti rājānā mitrāvaruṇā supāṇī |*  
> *āpaści dasya rodasī cidurvī ratnaṃ bhikṣaṃta savituḥ savāya‖ 7 ‖*

##### ॥ पदपाठः ॥ (Pada-pāṭha)

> त्रिः। आ। दिवः । सविता । सोषवीति । राजाना । मित्रावरुणा । सुपाणी इति सुपाणी ।  
> आपः । चित् । अस्य । रोदसी इति । चित् । उर्वी इति । रत्नं । भिक्षंत । सवितुः। सवाय॥

> *triḥ| ā| divaḥ | savitā | soṣavīti | rājānā | mitrāvaruṇā | supāṇī iti supāṇī |*  
> *āpaḥ | cit | asya | rodasī iti | cit | urvī iti | ratnaṃ | bhikṣaṃta | savituḥ| savāya‖*

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> सविता देवो दिवो दिवसस्य त्रिस्त्रिषु कालेष्टा सोषवीति । अस्मभ्यं धनान्यासुवतु । प्रेरयतु । किंच राजाना राजानौ सुपाणी कल्याणपाणी मित्रावरुणावापः।
> आप्पोति सर्वं जगदित्याप अंतरिक्षं । नित्यबहुवचनांतत्वादृहुवचनं । चिदपि च
> उर्वि विस्तीर्णे रोदसी द्यावापृथिव्यावेता देवताः सवितुः प्रेरकस्यास्य देवस्य
> सवाय सवेन प्रेरणेन रत्नमपेक्षितमर्थं भिक्षंत । याचंते ॥ सोसवीति । पू
> प्रेरण इत्यस्य यज्लुकि लटि रूपं । मित्रावरुणा । देवताद्वंद्वे चेत्युभयपदप्रकृतिस्वरत्वं । भिक्षंत । भिक्ष याज्ञायामित्यस्य लजि रूपं । सवाय । जवसव् च ।
> पा. ३-३-५६-४ । इत्यजंतत्वेन निपातनादंतोदात्तत्वं ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The god Savitṛ, three times (triḥ) each day (divaḥ), "soṣavīti": let him impel wealth to us. Further, the two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa, with fair hands (सुपाणी (*supāṇī*), "of auspicious hands"), the "āpaḥ," and the two broad ones, heaven and earth (रोदसी (*rodasī*)), these deities ask for what they want, "ratna," through the impelling (सवाय (*savāya*)) of this impelling god Savitṛ. "Āpaḥ" is the atmosphere, because it pervades (āpnoti) the whole world. It is a word that is always plural, hence the plural. "Cit" means "also." "Bhikṣanta" means "they ask."

### Printed p. 367

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- सविता (*savitā*)—the god Savitṛ
- दिवः (*divaḥ*)—of the day
- त्रिः (*triḥ*)—at the three times
- आ सोषवीति (*ā soṣavīti*)—may he supply wealth to us
- राजाना (*rājānā*)—the two lords of the world
- सुपाणी (*supāṇī*)—possessing excellent hands
- मित्रावरुणा (*mitrāvaruṇā*)—Mitra and Varuṇa
- आपः चित् (*āpaḥ cit*)—the atmosphere too
- उर्वि (*urvi*)—broad
- रोदसी (*rodasī*)—heaven and earth
- सवितुः (*savituḥ*)—of the impeller
- अस्य (*asya*)—of this god
- सवाय (*savāya*)—by the impelling
- रत्नं (*ratnaṃ*)—wealth
- भिक्षंत (*bhikṣaṃta*)—they ask

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

May the god Savitṛ supply us with wealth at the three times of the day. Mitra and Varuṇa, lords of the world and possessing excellent hands, the atmosphere, and the broad heaven and earth also ask for the wealth they desire from this impeller, Āditya.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
May Savitri bestow upon us wealth at the (three periods) of the day, for the well-handed Mitra and Varuna, the waters, the vast heaven and earth, solicit precious things from the liberality of Savitri.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

The present mantra praises Savitṛ: heaven and earth, Mitra and Varuṇa, and the other deities, known by epithets such as ऋतवाना (*ṛtavānā*), ऋतावृधः (*ṛtāvṛdhaḥ*) and राजाना (*rājānā*), look for Savitṛ's favour and perform their duties only by his impulsion. "उतेशिषे प्रसवस्य त्वमेक इत् (*uteśiṣe prasavasya tvameka it*)": you alone are the source and lord of the whole universe. Describing his position in this way, the mantra shows Savitṛ's greatness. What Savitṛ's place is in the sovereignty of the gods will be explained in the introduction to Ṛ. Saṃ. sūkta 3-62.

Mitra and Varuṇa have two epithets, राजाना (*rājānā*) and सुपाणी (*supāṇī*). These epithets show the nature of Mitra and Varuṇa. The nature of Mitra and Varuṇa is described in mantras such as ययोर्धाम धर्मणा रोचते बृहद्ययो रुभे रोदसी नाधसी वृत् (*yayordhāma dharmaṇā rocate bṛhadyayo rubhe rodasī nādhasī vṛt*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-65-5). They pervade the universe and shine of themselves, and they make the whole universe shine by their own light.

आपः (*āpaḥ*): आप्रोति सर्वं जगत् इत्यापः अंतरिक्षं (*āproti sarvaṃ jagat ityāpaḥ aṃtarikṣaṃ*). Because it pervades the whole world, the atmosphere has the name "āpaḥ." The Nirukta authors also include this word among the names of the atmosphere.

### Printed p. 368
In some places "āpaḥ" means the water in the atmosphere, but the intended sense is understood to be the atmosphere that is its support. In some places the question "what is āpaḥ?" appears in the Śruti text itself.

प्रजां धर्मेण दाधारैवमेते मनः पितरं परिचरंत्यापश्च वरुणश्च ० यावदन्वापो यावदनु वरुणस्तावानस्यलोको भवति नास्य तावल्लोको जीर्यते यावदेतेषां न जीर्यतेऽपां च वरुणस्य च य एवमेताः मनसो विभूतिं वेद । (*prajāṃ dharmeṇa dādhāraivamete manaḥ pitaraṃ paricaraṃtyāpaśca varuṇaśca 0 yāvadanvāpo yāvadanu varuṇastāvānasyaloko bhavati nāsya tāvalloko jīryate yāvadeteṣāṃ na jīryate 'pāṃ ca varuṇasya ca ya evametāḥ manaso vibhūtiṃ veda |*) (I. Ā. 2-1-7) **NOTE**

Prajāpati, described as the Supreme Person, created Varuṇa and Apaḥ (water) by his mental resolve alone. Water serves as a help to good works, Varuṇa watches over the order of creatures, and Prajāpati makes this resolve fruitful; so they attend on him. Since this is the description, there is room for the doubt as to what the principle "āpaḥ" is. Therefore:

आसा ३ इत्याप इति तदिदमाप एवेदं वै मूलमदस्तूलमयं पितैते पुत्रा यत्र ह क्व च पुत्रस्य तत्पितुः । (*āsā 3 ityāpa iti tadidamāpa evedaṃ vai mūlamadastūlamayaṃ pitaite putrā yatra ha kva ca putrasya tatpituḥ |*) (I. Ā. 2-1-8) **NOTE**

What is āpaḥ? What, in truth, is the nature of this principle? Its greatness is as follows: everything in the universe is pervaded by this water; it is the root cause of the creation of the universe, and the rest is its effect. The Person who is the support of this water-principle is the father. Since this is the description, it is understood that "āpaḥ" is not merely the atmosphere, but has a wider extent than the atmosphere. The etymology given in the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa also supports this view.

सेदग्ं सर्वमाप्नोत्यदिदं किं च यदाप्नोत्तस्मादापः ॥ (*sedagṃ sarvamāpnotyadidaṃ kiṃ ca yadāpnottasmādāpaḥ ‖*) (Śa. Patra 6-1-19) **NOTE**

The etymology is that what has the power to pervade everything is known by the name "āpaḥ." But what does it pervade? In some places it is said to pervade the whole universe, moving and unmoving, and not merely one fixed world such as the atmosphere. It is also taught that it is the Supreme Brahman principle.

स योऽपो ब्रह्मेत्युपास्त आप्नोति सर्वान्यामान् ॥ (*sa yo 'po brahmetyupāsta āpnoti sarvānyāmān ‖*) (Chā. U. 7-10-2)

It says that one who worships water as Brahman obtains all the aims of human life. But here it does not mean water as the complete Brahman. Water and fire are all parts of Brahman. Even so,

### Printed p. 369

Identity is stated; and it is also made known that the world of waters is a created world and not something existing before the creation of the universe:

आत्मा वा इदमेक एवाग्र आसीन्नान्यत्किंचन मिषत् । स ई क्षत । लोकान्नु सृजा इति । इमांल्लोकानसृजत । अंभोमरीचीर्मरमापः । (*ātmā vā idameka evāgra āsīnnānyatkiṃcana miṣat | sa ī kṣata | lokānnu sṛjā iti | imāṃllokānasṛjata | aṃbhomarīcīrmaramāpaḥ |*) (Ai. Ā. 9-4-1) **NOTE**

It says: before the creation of the universe only this principle of the Self existed; nothing else existed. Then, desiring the work of creation, it created these four worlds: Ambhaḥ, Marīci, Mara and Āpaḥ. Of these, Ambhaḥ is the heavenly world. [Ambhaḥ commonly means water, but in this quoted sentence it means the heavenly world, which lies above the atmosphere.] Marīci is the atmosphere pervaded by radiance. Mara, subject to death, is this earth. What lies below this is the world of waters (Āpaḥ). Ordinarily only the three divisions heaven, earth and atmosphere are well known, but here a fourth is added.

If such contexts are examined, a difference appears between the atmosphere as explained in the bhāṣya on the present Ṛk and the world called Āpaḥ explained in the quoted sentence. Even so, because of its pervasiveness the derivation of the word Āpaḥ fits both places. Whether it be the atmosphere or the world below the earth, the purport is that everything is nourished by the grace of Savitṛ.

उर्वी रोदसी (*urvī rodasī*)—the very extensive heaven and earth. From a gross point of view the epithet उर्वी (*urvī*) for the word रोदसी (*rodasī*) seems slightly unsuitable. The word उर्वी (*urvī*) means "very extended". रोदसी द्यावापृथिव्य विरोधनात् (*rodasī dyāvāpṛthivya virodhanāt*): because heaven and earth are bound and limited by a bounded limit (sīmā), they have the synonym रोदसी (*rodasī*). So the doubt arises naturally that the epithet उर्वी (*urvī*), which shows wide extent, cannot suit a world that is limited and bound. The Nirukta-author has read the word उर्वी (*urvī*) among the names of the earth and again among the names of "heaven and earth" (Ni. 1-1; 1-30). So it cannot be said that there is any incongruity here. Since the word रोदसी (*rodasī*) is here a synonym of heaven and earth, उर्वी (*urvī*) must be taken to mean "extended". It is a very meaningful word for indicating greatness and extent.

अयं मे पीत उदियर्ति वाचमयं मनीषामुशतीमजीगः । अयं षळुर्वीरमिमीत धीरो न याभ्यो भुवनं कच्चनारे ॥ (*ayaṃ me pīta udiyarti vācamayaṃ manīṣāmuśatīmajīgaḥ | ayaṃ ṣaḷurvīramimīta dhīro na yābhyo bhuvanaṃ kaccanāre ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-3)

### Printed p. 370

This King Soma has created the six Urvīs; no region in the world lies beyond these Urvīs. These six are all-pervading. When this is said, which are these six Urvīs? They are the earth, the heavenly world, day, night, the waters and the plants. How? In the Śatapatha mantra

षण्मोर्वीर्गंहसस्पांत्वग्निश्च पृथिवी चापश्च वाजश्च रात्रिश्चेता मा देवताः (*ṣaṇmorvīrgaṃhasaspāṃtvagniśca pṛthivī cāpaśca vājaśca rātriścetā mā devatāḥ*) (Śa. Brā. 1-5-1-22)

there is an enumeration of which these Urvīs are. On this basis Sāyaṇa quoted this Brāhmaṇa sentence and explained as stated above. The same is continued and explained in the Ṛk-saṃhitā too; each Urvī is described with an epithet.

अयं स यो वरिमाणं पृथिव्या वर्षाणं दिवो अकृणोदयं सः । अयं पीयूषं त्रिसृषु प्रवत्सु सोमो दाधारोर्वं १ तरिक्षं ॥ अयं विदच्चित्रदृशीकमर्णः शुक्रसद्मनामुषसामनीके । अयं महान्महता स्यंभनेनोद्द्यामस्तभ्नाद्वषभो मरुत्वान् ॥ (*ayaṃ sa yo varimāṇaṃ pṛthivyā varṣāṇaṃ divo akṛṇodayaṃ saḥ | ayaṃ pīyūṣaṃ trisṛṣu pravatsu somo dādhārorvaṃ 1 tarikṣaṃ ‖ ayaṃ vidaccitradṛśīkamarṇaḥ śukrasadmanāmuṣasāmanīke | ayaṃ mahānmahatā syaṃbhanenoddyāmastabhnādvaṣabho marutvān ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-4, 5)

This Soma made the extent of the earth still greater; he increased the height of the heavenly world; he caused the three kinds of plants to spread throughout the universe; he increased the very extended atmosphere; he lit the world-attracting light of the sun endlessly; likewise he caused the middle world to become extended; and so on: the extension of all the worlds indicated by the word उर्वी (*urvī*) is described. Besides:

आ यः पप्र जायमान उर्वी दूरेदृशा भासा कृष्णाध्वा । (*ā yaḥ papra jāyamāna urvī dūredṛśā bhāsā kṛṣṇādhvā |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-10-4)

Agni, whose path is black, as soon as he was born pervaded the very extended Urvīs, that is, all of heaven and earth. Here the word Urvī is a synonym for heaven and earth only; or it may be a synonym for the earth alone. For example:

उर्वाः पदो नि दधाति सानौ रिंहत्योधो अरुषासो अस्य ॥ (*urvāḥ pado ni dadhāti sānau riṃhatyodho aruṣāso asya ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-146-2)

Agni sets his foot on the altar of the earth, very extended and high like a peak; so here the word Urvī indicates the earth alone.

Thus, when the word Urvī indicates endless extension, is this epithet fitting for Rodasī, which has a fixed limit? Here it may be said that the epithet is entirely proper.

### Printed p. 371

How? The etymology विरोधनाद्रोदसी (*virodhanādrodasī*) can be given only in one context; the pervasiveness to be indicated by the word रोदसी (*rodasī*) is itself well known. With this purport, when describing the nature of the Aśvin deities too (?), because this pervasiveness exists, identity of the Aśvin deities with heaven and earth is stated. **NOTE**

अथ यदश्विनावितीमे ह वै द्यावापृथिवी प्रत्यक्षमश्विनाविमे हीदग्ंसर्वमाश्नुनातां पुष्करस्रजावित्यग्निरेवास्यै पुष्करमादित्योऽमुष्यै (*atha yadaśvināvitīme ha vai dyāvāpṛthivī pratyakṣamaśvināvime hīdagṃsarvamāśnunātāṃ puṣkarasrajāvityagnirevāsyai puṣkaramādityo 'muṣyai*) (Śa. Brā. 4-1-5-16)

The Aśvin deities are directly manifest in this very form of heaven and earth. Because they have a nature that pervades every region, they have this name. They are called Puṣkara-srajas. Agni and Āditya are these Puṣkaras: Agni is the lotus (puṣkara) of the earth, Āditya that of the heavenly world.

शौर्णवाभोः दृच्छेत्वस्मिन् अश्विनौ मन्यते स्तुता । अहोरात्रौ च तावेव स्यातां तावेन रोदसी ॥ (*śaurṇavābhoḥ dṛcchetvasmin aśvinau manyate stutā | ahorātrau ca tāveva syātāṃ tāvena rodasī ‖*) (Bṛ. De. 7-126)

An opinion that this very heaven and earth, well known as Rodasī, are also well known as the Aśvin deities has been cited in the Bṛhaddevatā and other works. It is because of this attribute of pervasiveness that the name arises; therefore the epithet उर्वी (*urvī*) is proper.

The word रोदसी (*rodasī*) is used in the dual, but in some places it is also used in the singular. In those contexts it is not easy to say definitely what it means. In some cases the word occurs in one and the same mantra in both the first half and the second half; then a different meaning has to be given for each occurrence. For example:

इदुग्राः शवसा धृष्णुषेणा उभे युजंत रोदसी सुमेके ! अध स्मैषु रोदसी स्वशोचिरामवत्सु तस्थौ न रोकः ॥ (*idugrāḥ śavasā dhṛṣṇuṣeṇā ubhe yujaṃta rodasī sumeke ! adha smaiṣu rodasī svaśocirāmavatsu tasthau na rokaḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-66-6)

This mantra praises the Maruts. The meaning of the first sentence is that these Maruts yoke both heaven and earth; and the meaning of the second sentence is that Rodasī unites her radiance in these Maruts. But who is this Rodasī? Sāyaṇa has explained it as the middle speech (mādhyamikā vāk). One view is that this Rodasī is the wife of Rudra.

### Printed p. 372

Another view is that she is the wife of the Maruts. "Wife of Rudra" means the mother of the Maruts. Rudra is Vāyu. This wife of Vāyu is the middle speech. The radiance in the form of lightning in that speech, joined with thunder, is called Rodasī. Supporting this very view:

रोदसी देवपत्नीनां अथर्वांगिरसे यथा (*rodasī devapatnīnāṃ atharvāṃgirase yathā*) (Bṛ. De. 2-143)

According to the Atharvāṅgirasa view, Rodasī is one of the wives of the gods: here is an example with the singular used. Even in such places, since the attribute of pervasiveness is present, the epithet उर्वी (*urvī*) is natural. In the present mantra the meaning is: heaven and earth, very extended and all-pervading.

सवितुः (*savituḥ*)—सवाय (*savāya*)—these two words also describe the nature of Savitṛ. Because he is the impeller of the world, the impelling function of the deity known by the word Savitṛ is described by these words. This attribute of Savitṛ will be explained further on. Mitra and Varuṇa, and heaven and earth, though they are purifiers of the world, maintainers of the world's order, givers of wealth and possessed of the highest greatness, all have their activity accomplished only by the impulsion of this Savitṛ: this is the purport of the description.

> दूणशा दुर्नशा केनापि विनाशयितुमशक्यानि रोचनानि दीप्यमानानि त्रिस्त्रिण्यंतमानि स्थानानि संति । एतेषु त्रिषु स्थानेष्टसुरस्य । अस्यति क्षिपति सर्वमित्यसुरः

> शोभंते । तानेव विशिनष्टि । ऋतावानः । ऋतं सत्यभूतमग्निहोत्रादिकं कर्म

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

दूणशा (*dūṇaśā*) is दुर्नशा (*durnaśā*): the bright (रोचनानि (*rocanāni*), shining) places, that cannot be destroyed by anyone, are three in number, the highest. In these three places there are the sons (वीराः (*vīrāḥ*)) of the Asura. Asura is he who throws out (अस्यति (*asyati*)) everything: the year, whose nature is Time. His three sons, in the forms of Agni, Vāyu and Sūrya, shine. He now qualifies them: ऋतावानः (*ṛtāvānaḥ*); ऋतं (*ṛtaṃ*) is the rite such as the Agnihotra, which is true (the text breaks off here and continues on the next page).

### Printed p. 373

> तद्वंतः । इषिरा यज्ञार्थं शीघ्रगतिमंतो दूळभासो दुर्दभासः केनापि स्वतेजसा तिरस्कर्तुमशक्या एते सर्वे देवा विदथेऽस्मदीये यज्ञे दिवोऽह्नः संबंधिषु
> त्रिस्त्रिषु सवनेष्वा संतु । समंताद्यजनीयतया भवंतु ॥ उत्तमा । उत्तमशश्वत्तमौ
> सर्वत्रेत्युंभादिषु पाठादंतोदात्तत्वं । दूणशा । नशेः कृच्छार्थे खल् । दुरो
> दाशनाशदभेषूत्वं वक्तव्यमिति रेफस्योत्वं । उत्तरपदादेः ष्टुत्वं । लित्स्वरः ।
> दूळभासः । पूर्ववदुत्वष्टुत्वे ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

(Continuing) Those who possess it (the ṛta). इषिरा (*iṣirā*): swift-moving for the sacrifice. दूळभासः (*dūḷabhāsaḥ*) is दुर्दभासः (*durdabhāsaḥ*): that cannot be overcome by anyone with his own radiance. May all these deities be present at our sacrifice (विदथे (*vidathe*)), in each of the three libations belonging to the day (दिवः (*divaḥ*)): that is, may they be there on all sides as worthy of worship. (The rest of the block is grammar.)

##### प्रतिपदार्थ (Pratipadārtha)

- दूणशा (*dūṇaśā*)—beyond destruction
- रोचनानि (*rocanāni*)—shining
- उत्तमा त्रिः (*uttamā triḥ*)—there are three highest places (in these places)
- असुरस्य (*asurasya*)—of the year, whose nature is time
- वीराः त्रयः (*vīrāḥ trayaḥ*)—the three sons in the forms of Agni, Vāyu and Sūrya
- राजंति (*rājaṃti*)—shine
- ऋतावानः (*ṛtāvānaḥ*)—those whose rite is of the nature of truth
- इषिरः (*iṣiraḥ*)—swift-moving for the sacrifice
- दूळभासः (*dūḷabhāsaḥ*)—those whose radiance cannot be checked
- देवाः (*devāḥ*)—the deities
- विदथे (*vidathe*)—in the sacrifices
- दिवः (*divaḥ*)—of each day
- त्रिः (*triḥ*)—also at the time of the three libations
- आ संतु (*ā saṃtu*)—may they come as worthy of worship and sit

##### भावार्थ (Bhāvārtha)

There are three highest places, beyond destruction and shining. In these places Agni, Vāyu and Sūrya, the sons in form of the year whose nature is time, shine. May the deities, whose rite is of the nature of truth, who are swift-moving for the sacrifice and whose radiance cannot be checked, come in the sacrifices, at the times of the three libations of each day too, as worthy of worship, and sit.

##### English translation (H. H. Wilson)
Three are the excellent uninjurable bright regions, three scions of the powerful (year) are shining; practisers of truth, quick-moving of surpassing radiance: may the deities be present thrice daily at the sacrifice.

##### विशेषविषयगळु (Special Topics)

In the present mantra the three worlds beginning with the earth, and the greatness of the presiding deities of the three worlds, Agni and the others, are praised. To make known the nature of the three worlds indicated by त्रिः (*triḥ*) there are three epithets: दूणशा (*dūṇaśā*), रोचनानि (*rocanāni*), उत्तमा (*uttamā*). The bhāṣya does not specify which the highest places are. But वीराः त्रयः (*vīrāḥ trayaḥ*) must be understood as the worlds of Agni, Vāyu and heaven. Ordinarily these worlds are often specified by epithets that show their individual peculiarity.

### Printed p. 374

For example: उर्वि (*urvi*), पृथिवी (*pṛthivī*), अपरा (*aparā*) and the like show the extent of the earth; भूमिः (*bhūmiḥ*) shows that the earth is the place of origin for beings; मही (*mahī*), उत्ताना (*uttānā*) and the like show its height. In many places the earth is indicated merely by the word इदं (*idaṃ*); in such contexts it means what is distinct from the worlds above. Epithets such as दिवि (*divi*), रोचन (*rocana*), व्योम (*vyoma*) describe the radiance of the atmosphere; सानु (*sānu*), विष्टप (*viṣṭapa*), पृष्ठ (*pṛṣṭha*) indicate its height. In some places it is even hard to say what the difference between the atmosphere and the heavenly world is. For example, if there is a difference between atmosphere and heaven (द्यौः (*dyauḥ*)), it is hard to say whether the word रोदसी (*rodasī*) means earth and atmosphere or heaven and earth.

The epithet or synonym रजस् (*rajas*) often indicates the atmosphere. But, just as in the present Ṛk there is the epithet उत्तमा (*uttamā*), रजस् (*rajas*) too is a word that can indicate the three worlds. In such contexts the epithets तृतीय (*tṛtīya*), उत्तम (*uttama*), परम (*parama*) tell which of the three worlds is meant; but there too one must say according to the context. For example:

सहस्रधारेव ता असश्च तस्य तीये संतु रजसि प्रजावतीः । (*sahasradhāreva tā asaśca tasya tīye saṃtu rajasi prajāvatīḥ |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-74-6)

Here तृतीये रजसि (*tṛtīye rajasi*) is explained as heaven; one may say the heavenly world.

समुद्रे त्वा नृमणा अप्पं १ तर्नृचक्षा ईधे दिवो अग्न ऊधन् । तृतीये त्वा रजसि तस्थिवांसमपामुपस्थे महिषा अवर्धन् ॥ (*samudre tvā nṛmaṇā appaṃ 1 tarnṛcakṣā īdhe divo agna ūdhan | tṛtīye tvā rajasi tasthivāṃsamapāmupasthe mahiṣā avardhan ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-45-3)

Here there is the word दिवः (*divaḥ*) indicating the heavenly world. In this context तृतीये रजसि (*tṛtīye rajasi*) is explained as the atmosphere. The word तृतीय (*tṛtīya*) is not explained as "the third world" but explained otherwise. In उतेदमुत्तमं रजः (*utedamuttamaṃ rajaḥ*) (9-22-5) the "highest region" is understood as the heavenly world.

तिस्रो द्यावो निहिता अंतरस्मिंस्तिस्रो भूमीरुपराः षड्विधानाः । गृत्सो राजा वरुणश्चक्र एतं दिवि प्रेंखं हिरण्ययं शुभे कं ॥ (*tisro dyāvo nihitā aṃtarasmiṃstisro bhūmīruparāḥ ṣaḍvidhānāḥ | gṛtso rājā varuṇaścakra etaṃ divi preṃkhaṃ hiraṇyayaṃ śubhe kaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-87-5)

Here, as stated earlier in the mantra त्रिपाजस्यः (*tripājasyaḥ*) of the present sūkta (3-56-3), the heavenly world and the earth are shown as threefold by तिस्रः द्यावः (*tisraḥ dyāvaḥ*) and तिस्रः भूमीः (*tisraḥ bhūmīḥ*), and the atmosphere is stated in the singular. It is also a special feature that दिवि (*divi*) is used as a synonym of the atmosphere.

### Printed p. 375

त्रिरश्विना सिंधुभिः सप्तमातृभिस्त्रय आहवास्त्रेधा हविष्कृतं । तिस्रः पृथिवीरुपरि प्रवा दिवो नाकं रक्षेथे द्युभिरक्तुभिर्हितं ॥ (*triraśvinā siṃdhubhiḥ saptamātṛbhistraya āhavāstredhā haviṣkṛtaṃ | tisraḥ pṛthivīrupari pravā divo nākaṃ rakṣethe dyubhiraktubhirhitaṃ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-34-8)

Here the word नाक (*nāka*) indicates the fourth world. "पृथिव्यादिलोकेभ्यः ऊर्ध्वं आदित्यलोकं (*pṛthivyādilokebhyaḥ ūrdhvaṃ ādityalokaṃ*)": it is explained as the world of Āditya lying above the three worlds beginning with the earth. In many places the fourth world is described, as shown by the contexts. For example:

चमूषच्छेनः शकुनो विभृत्वा गोविंदुर्द्रप्स आयुधानि बिभ्रत् । अपामूर्मिं सचमानः समुद्रं तुरीयं धाम महिषो विवक्ति ॥ (*camūṣacchenaḥ śakuno vibhṛtvā goviṃdurdrapsa āyudhāni bibhrat | apāmūrmiṃ sacamānaḥ samudraṃ turīyaṃ dhāma mahiṣo vivakti ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-96-19)

King Soma, having traversed the entire atmosphere, then entered the fourth abode (तुरीयधाम (*turīyadhāma*)) and moved about there: thus it is made known that the fourth world is beyond the well-known three worlds, and that it is the world of Āditya. The greatness of this fourth world will be shown later when the Gāyatrī mantra is explained; here only its distinctness may be noted. Sāyaṇa here says तुरीयं चतुर्थं धाम चांद्रमसं स्थानं सेवते । सूरलोकस्योपरि चंद्रमसः लोकः विद्यते । (*turīyaṃ caturthaṃ dhāma cāṃdramasaṃ sthānaṃ sevate | sūralokasyopari caṃdramasaḥ lokaḥ vidyate |*), that is, that this fourth world is known as the world of the moon and is beyond the solar world. But that this fourth world is described as the world of Āditya in the Upaniṣads and other works may be examined later. Even where it says तिस्रः पृथिवीः त्रीणि रोचना (*tisraḥ pṛthivīḥ trīṇi rocanā*), the meaning has to be given according to the context.

त्रिरुत्तराणि पप्रतुर्वरुणस्य ध्रुवं सदः स सप्तानामिरज्यति नभंतामन्यके समे । (*triruttarāṇi papraturvaruṇasya dhruvaṃ sadaḥ sa saptānāmirajyati nabhaṃtāmanyake same |*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-41-9)

Here it is said that the rays of Varuṇa pervaded not only the three earths but, passing beyond them, the three highest worlds (उत्तराणि त्रिः (*uttarāṇi triḥ*)): a threefold world beyond the worlds beginning with the earth. Descriptions such as तिस्रः परावतो दिवः (*tisraḥ parāvato divaḥ*) (8-5 8) indicate the same point. **NOTE**. One of the mantras that give room for disagreement may be taken as an example and examined.

तिस्रो द्यावः सवितुर्दा उपस्था एका यमस्य भुवने विराषाट् । आणिं न रथ्यममृताधि तस्थुरिह ब्रवीतु य उ तच्छिकेतत् ॥ (*tisro dyāvaḥ saviturdā upasthā ekā yamasya bhuvane virāṣāṭ | āṇiṃ na rathyamamṛtādhi tasthuriha bravītu ya u tacchiketat ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-35-6)

Of the three kinds of heavenly worlds, two belong to Savitṛ and one to Yama. Just as all the parts of a chariot rest on the linchpin and are joined depending on it, all the deathless worlds on this (the text breaks off here and the next window continues it).

### Printed p. 376

## Special Topics (continued)

…rest upon the world of Savitṛ alone. In Mādhava's commentary on the Ṛgveda, and in Sāyaṇa's commentary as well, these three worlds are explained as earth, atmosphere and heaven; of these, earth and heaven belong to Savitṛ, and the atmosphere is the world of Yama. Veṅkaṭamādhava, however, has explained that all three are varieties of the heavenly world, and that Agni and Savitṛ are the presiding deities of them. Skandasvāmin holds that either of these two opinions may be accepted.

There is a doubt also about the true meaning of तद्विष्णोः परमं पदं (*tadviṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padaṃ*), तुरीयं धाम (*turīyaṃ dhāma*) and the like. Yāska regards Viṣṇu as a deity of the heavenly region. But if the explanation in the Ṛksaṃhitā is examined, it appears that this heavenly region lies beyond the three worlds. In तिस्रो द्यावः (*tisro dyāvaḥ*), one is the seat of Soma and the Ṛbhus; the second is the world of Sūra; the third is the world of Āditya. That is the highest step of Viṣṇu.

In the present verse, even when त्रिः उत्तमा रोचना (*triḥ uttamā rocanā*) is taken as "three highest places", there is room for doubt. But since वीराः त्रयः (*vīrāḥ trayaḥ*) has been explained as Agni, Vāyu and Āditya, on that basis one has to say: earth, atmosphere and heaven.

दूणशा (*dūṇaśā*) may be explained as "that which is without destruction"; or it may also be explained as "that which cannot be obtained easily".

असुरस्य (*asurasya*)—अस्यति क्षिपति सर्वमित्यसुरः । कालात्मा संवत्सरः । (*asyati kṣipati sarvamityasuraḥ | kālātmā saṃvatsaraḥ |*) Here only one aspect of the year is indicated: the year in the form of Time, which holds everything under its control. As the year is the cause of creation and growth, so it is the cause of decay. As explained before, here too Prajāpati, the presiding deity of the year, may be what is meant.

प्रजापतिर्लोकानभ्यतपत्तेषां तप्यमानानां रसान्प्रावृहदग्निं पृथिव्या वायुमंतरिक्षादादित्यं दिवः ॥ (*prajāpatirlokānabhyatapatteṣāṃ tapyamānānāṃ rasānprāvṛhadagniṃ pṛthivyā vāyumaṃtarikṣādādityaṃ divaḥ ‖*) (Bhā. U. 4-17-1)**NOTE**

Prajāpati meditated on the essence of the three worlds, drew out their sap and spread it forth. From the earth he caused Agni to shine, from the atmosphere Vāyu, from heaven Āditya. Since it is thus described that from the three worlds spoken of in the present Ṛk as रोचना त्रिः (*rocanā triḥ*) he caused three excellent deities to shine, here also असुरस्य (*asurasya*) may be said to mean Prajāpati in the form of the year.

The word asura denotes a special power; this power may be nourishing or it may be destroying. Although the special meanings of this word were given earlier, in the present context one must determine its import and examine its etymology closely, in order to know of which principle, and of what forms of power, this word shows.

### Printed p. 377

Its etymology must be understood in detail.

असुरा असुरताः स्थानेष्वस्ताः स्थानेभ्य इति वा । अपि वा असुरिति प्राणनाम अस्तः शरीरे भवति तेन तद्वंतः ॥ (*asurā asuratāḥ sthāneṣvastāḥ sthānebhya iti vā | api vā asuriti prāṇanāma astaḥ śarīre bhavati tena tadvaṃtaḥ ‖*) (Ni. 3-8)

The rākṣasas are well known by the name asura because they are always satisfied with evil deeds. Or they may be asuras because they were cast out and thrust aside by the gods. Or the word asu may be a synonym of breath. Or there is the division that the gods are suras, because they were created by su, that is, by right conduct (sad-dharma), and the rākṣasas are a-suras, created by wrong conduct (a-su). For the present this explanation is irrelevant. The mantras of the preceding sūkta show what quality is indicated by the use of the word asura in the present context. महद्देवानामसुरत्वमेकं (*mahaddevānāmasuratvamekaṃ*) is the last pāda of every mantra of the preceding sūkta. In these places also, as in the etymology given in the present Ṛk, अस्यति क्षिपति सर्वानित्यसुरः प्रबलः । तस्य भावः असुरत्वं प्राबल्यं । महदैश्वर्यं । (*asyati kṣipati sarvānityasuraḥ prabalaḥ | tasya bhāvaḥ asuratvaṃ prābalyaṃ | mahadaiśvaryaṃ |*) is the explanation; the meaning is "lordship possessed of the power to subdue enemies". Therefore, when the asura-hood of individual gods has so much power, it need not be said that the asura-hood of Prajāpati, who is the lord of all the gods, is that which governs the universe. Because of this power of governing the universe, Prajāpati, or the Lord in the form of Time, is the one denoted by the word asura. In this governing of the universe, besides the work of mere accomplishing, the power that gives life to the whole universe is also manifested. Describing this power, there is in Ṛks such as

वि सुपर्णो अंतरिक्षाण्यख्यद्धभीरवेपाः असुरः सुनीथः (*vi suparṇo aṃtarikṣāṇyakhyaddhabhīravepāḥ asuraḥ sunīthaḥ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-35-7)

a description of the god who gives life to the universe. Since it is praised in the Brāhmaṇas and elsewhere that सर्वॆषां भूतानां प्राणानादायोदेति (*sarvèṣāṃ bhūtānāṃ prāṇānādāyodeti*) (Tai. Ā. 1-14-1)—Āditya is the giver of life to all beings—it is understood from the quoted mantra that the word asura here is an epithet of Āditya, who has that same power. Moreover, in places such as जनानां यो असुरो विधर्ता (*janānāṃ yo asuro vidhartā*) (7-56-24) the word is also explained as "possessed of wisdom". Thus a quality joined with various powers is described by the word asura. Since all powers—the power of creation, the power of destruction, the power of governing the universe and so on—are centred in Prajāpati in the form of Time, in the present context Prajāpati, the father of the whole universe including gods and men, may be the one denoted by the word asura. Since Prajāpati, Time and the year are synonyms in many contexts, whichever of them is used, there is no difference in the principle.

### Printed p. 378

एष वै मृत्युरत्यंवत्सरः । एष हि मर्त्यानामहोरात्राभ्यामायुः क्षिणोत्यथ म्रियंते तस्मादेष एव मृत्युः स यो हैतं मृत्युग्ं संवत्सरं वेद .... .... तस्मादेष एवांतकः स यो हैतमंतकं मृत्युग्ं संवत्सरं वेद न हास्यैष.... .... । ते देवाः एतस्मादंतकान्मै त्र्योः संवत्सरात्पजापतेर्बिभियां चक्रुः ॥ (*eṣa vai mṛtyuratyaṃvatsaraḥ | eṣa hi martyānāmahorātrābhyāmāyuḥ kṣiṇotyatha mriyaṃte tasmādeṣa eva mṛtyuḥ sa yo haitaṃ mṛtyugṃ saṃvatsaraṃ veda .... .... tasmādeṣa evāṃtakaḥ sa yo haitamaṃtakaṃ mṛtyugṃ saṃvatsaraṃ veda na hāsyaiṣa.... .... | te devāḥ etasmādaṃtakānmai tryoḥ saṃvatsarātpajāpaterbibhiyāṃ cakruḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 1C-4-3-1-3)**NOTE**

The great principle which, having attained asura-hood, holds the universe under its control by that power, and which Sāyaṇa has explained as अस्यति क्षिपति सर्वं (*asyati kṣipati sarvaṃ*)—कालात्मा संवत्सरः (*kālātmā saṃvatsaraḥ*), that great principle of the year is Prajāpati. As it is the source of the creation of the universe, so it is the source of its destruction. This year is Death. For human and other beings it makes life wear away (pass away) in the form of days and nights. It causes death to all. Therefore this year, in the form of Time, is the ender of all. It is described that even the gods, knowing the nature of this Prajāpati in the form of the year as the ender, became afraid.

Therefore, प्रजापतिर्वा इदमग्र आसीत् । स इमांस्त्रीन् लोकानभितताप । तेभ्यस्तप्तेभ्यस्त्रिणि ज्योतीग्‌ष्यजायंताग्निर्योऽयं पवते सूरः ॥ (*prajāpatirvā idamagra āsīt | sa imāṃstrīn lokānabhitatāpa | tebhyastaptebhyastriṇi jyotīgṣyajāyaṃtāgniryo 'yaṃ pavate sūraḥ ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 11-5 8-2)**NOTE** — The Prajāpati who is described thus: from Prajāpati, who existed before the creation of the universe, the three worlds beginning with earth were created, and from them the three luminous forms Agni, Vāyu and Āditya were created; who is described as the year that creates, and as Time, which though destroying is in the form of the year, and as the ender—the three sons of that Prajāpati, Agni, Vāyu and Āditya, in the form of three lights, are described in the present Ṛk as त्रयः वीराः (*trayaḥ vīrāḥ*).

ऋतावानः (*ṛtāvānaḥ*)—those who maintain the truth of the three worlds. Agni maintains the rules of sacrifice and the like on earth and so keeps truth in being. In the same way Vāyu, in the form of the life-breath of the universe, maintains the truth of the atmosphere, the giving of rain and so on. Āditya, being lord of these two worlds, maintains the truth of all the worlds; therefore the epithet ऋतावानः (*ṛtāvānaḥ*) applies to all together.

दूळभासः (*dūḷabhāsaḥ*)—दुःदभासः (*duḥdabhāsaḥ*): a radiance that no one has the power to restrain. By this epithet is described the nature of the radiances of Āditya, which are unlike others, supernatural, unobstructed and all-pervading.

## Sūkta 57 (Maṇḍala 3)

#### Ṛk 1

##### ॥ सायणभाष्यम् ॥ (Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya)

> प्र मे विविक्वानिति षडृचं चतुर्थं सूक्तं । विश्वामित्र ऋषिः । तिष्टप् छंदः ।
> विश्वे देवा देवता । अत्रानुक्रमणिका । प्र मे षळिति । सूक्तविनियोगो लैंगिकः ॥
> अनुवादवु—प्र मे विविक्वान् ऎंब ई सूक्तवु ऐदनॆय अनुवाकदल्लि नाल्कनॆय
> सूक्तवु. इदरल्लि आरु ऋक्कुगळिरुववु. ई सूक्तक्कॆ विश्वामित्रनु ऋषियु ; विश्वेदेवतॆगळु
> देवतॆयु ; त्रिष्टुप् छंदस्सु. अनुक्रमणिकॆयल्लि—प्र मे षट् ऎंदु हेळिरुवुदु. सूक्तद
> विनियोगवु लैंगिकवु.
> ॥ ओं ॥
> सूक्त—५७
> मंडल—३ ॥ अनुवाक—५ ॥ सूक्त—५७ ॥
> अष्टक—३ ॥ अध्याय—४ ॥ वर्ग—२ ॥
> ॥ सूक्तदल्लिरुव ऋक्संख्यॆ—६ ॥
> ऋषिः—विश्वामित्रः ॥
> देवता—विश्वे देवाः ॥
> छंदः—त्रिष्टुप् ॥

##### Gist of the bhāṣya

The sūkta beginning प्र मे विविक्वान् (*pra me vivikvān*) is the fourth sūkta (of the fifth anuvāka), of six Ṛks. The seer is Viśvāmitra, the deity the Viśvedevas, the metre Triṣṭubh. The Anukramaṇikā says प्र मे षळिति (*pra me ṣaḷiti*). The application (viniyoga) of the sūkta is by indication (liṅga). The Kannada gives: Maṇḍala 3, Anuvāka 5, Sūkta 57; Aṣṭaka 3, Adhyāya 4, Varga 2; number of Ṛks in the sūkta 6.

##### ॥ संहितापाठः ॥ (Saṃhitā-pāṭha)

> प्र मे॑ विवि॒क्त्वा अ॑विदन्मनी॒षां धे॒नुं चरं॑तीं॒ प्रयु॑ता॒मगो॑पां ।  
> स॒द्यश्चि॒द्या दु॑दु॒हे भूरि॑ धा॒सेरिंद्र॒स्तद॒ग्निः प॑नि॒तारो॑ अस्याः ॥

> *pra me viviktvā avidanmanīṣāṃ dhenuṃ caraṃtīṃ prayutāmagopāṃ |*
