Brā. 13-28).

गायत्री कनिष्ठा छंदसागं सती यज्ञमुखं परीयाय । (*gāyatrī kaniṣṭhā chaṃdasāgaṃ satī yajñamukhaṃ parīyāya |*) (Tai. Saṃ. 6-1-6-3)

अधातः शिरः । तद्दायत्रीषु भवत्यग्रं वै छंदसां गायत्र्यग्रमंगानां शिरः । (*adhātaḥ śiraḥ | taddāyatrīṣu bhavatyagraṃ vai chaṃdasāṃ gāyatryagramaṃgānāṃ śiraḥ |*) (Ai. Ā. 1-4-1)

It is stated that just as the head is the chief of all the limbs of the body, so the Gāyatrī is the chief of all metres, and that afterwards the remaining metres were constructed on its basis. For this very reason गायत्री छंदसां माता (*gāyatrī chaṃdasāṃ mātā*) (Tai. U. 4-15-1) **NOTE**: the Gāyatrī is praised as the mother of all metres. All the other metres are formed on the basis of this metre. In the Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya (Ai. Ā. 10-4-1) **NOTE** there is the explanation, for the Aitareya Āraṇyaka sentence छंदसां माता (*chaṃdasāṃ mātā*), that the other metres are constructed on its basis: इतरेषां छंदसामस्यॆव चतुश्चतुरक्षराधिक्येन तत्तच्छंदोभिः प्रतिमिवीते ॥ (*itareṣāṃ chaṃdasāmasyèva catuścaturakṣarādhikyena tattacchaṃdobhiḥ pratimivīte ‖*) How this is so: if the Gāyatrī metre has twenty-four syllables—

Uṣṇik 24+4 = 28
Anuṣṭubh 24+4+4 = 32
Bṛhatī 24+4+4+4 = 36
Paṅkti 24+4+4+4+4+4 = 40 **NOTE**

### Printed p. 586

Triṣṭup: 24+4+4+4+4+4 = 44.
Jagatī: 24+4+4+4+4+4+4 = 48.

The purport is that, taking the Gāyatrī as the base, the Uṣṇik and the rest are formed by adding four syllables each time. Moreover, Agni is the chief of all sacrifices, and the Gāyatrī metre is a synonym of Agni, so it is the head of all (the metres).

. गायत्रं पुरस्ताद्गायति । अग्निर्वैगायत्रमग्निमेवास्यैतच्छिरः करोत्यथो शिरः ॥ ( (*. gāyatraṃ purastādgāyati | agnirvaigāyatramagnimevāsyaitacchiraḥ karotyatho śiraḥ ‖ (*) (Śa. Brā. 9-1-2-35)

Thus its primacy is praised.

शिरो वै यज्ञ स्यातिथ्यं सवाक्षरा वै गायत्री अष्टौ तानि यान्यन्वाह प्रणवो नवमः पूर्वार्धो वै यज्ञस्य गायत्री ॥ (*śiro vai yajña syātithyaṃ savākṣarā vai gāyatrī aṣṭau tāni yānyanvāha praṇavo navamaḥ pūrvārdho vai yajñasya gāyatrī ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 3-4-1-15)

The Gāyatrī consists of nine syllables. The praṇava is one; the other eight belong to the Gāyatrī that is its root form. The Gāyatrī is the chief of the whole sacrifice. Why? Because:

यो गायत्रीं हरिणीं ।.... यजमानग्ग् स्वर्गं लोकमभिवहंतीं । (*yo gāyatrīṃ hariṇīṃ |.... yajamānagg svargaṃ lokamabhivahaṃtīṃ |*) (Śa. Brā. 11-4-1-8)

Such a meritorious Gāyatrī is praised as carrying the sacrificer to heaven. Such is the power of the Gāyatrī.

**The Gāyatrī pervades all the savanas**

Śaṅkarācārya has shown a third point to prove that the Gāyatrī plays the most important part in the sacrifice: सर्वसवनव्यापकत्वाच्छ यज्ञस्य प्राधान्यं गायत्र्याः (*sarvasavanavyāpakatvāccha yajñasya prādhānyaṃ gāyatryāḥ*). In these three rites too, the Prātaḥsavana, the Mādhyandinasavana and the Tṛtīyasavana, the help of the Gāyatrī is absolutely necessary for performing the prescribed work; this is known from Brāhmaṇa and other passages.

गायत्री वै प्रातःसवनं वहति । त्रिष्टुप्माध्यंदिनग्ंसवनं जगतीतृतीयसवनं तद्वा अनेकाकिन्येव त्रिष्टुप्माध्यंदिनग्ंसवनं वहति गायत्रा च बृहत्या चानेकाकिनी जगतीतृतीयसवनं गायत्रोष्ठिहककुभ्यामनुष्टुभा । गायत्रैवैकाकिनी प्रातःसवनं वहति । (*gāyatrī vai prātaḥsavanaṃ vahati | triṣṭupmādhyaṃdinagṃsavanaṃ jagatītṛtīyasavanaṃ tadvā anekākinyeva triṣṭupmādhyaṃdinagṃsavanaṃ vahati gāyatrā ca bṛhatyā cānekākinī jagatītṛtīyasavanaṃ gāyatroṣṭhihakakubhyāmanuṣṭubhā | gāyatraivaikākinī prātaḥsavanaṃ vahati |*) (Śa. Brā. 4-2-4-10)

The Gāyatrī carries the Prātaḥsavana, the Triṣṭup the Mādhyandinasavana, and the Jagatī the Tṛtīyasavana. But the Triṣṭup cannot carry the Mādhyandinasavana without the help of the Gāyatrī. Only when the Gāyatrī, joined with the Bṛhatī,

### Printed p. 587

helps the Triṣṭup can it do so. In the same way the Jagatī too cannot carry the Tṛtīyasavana without the help of the Gāyatrī; it can do so only with the help of the Gāyatrī joined with the Kakubh and the Uṣṇik. But the Gāyatrī alone can carry the Prātaḥsavana without seeking the help of any other metre. Because the Gāyatrī pervades all the savanas, it has primacy in the sacrifice.

The question may be asked: although the Triṣṭup has eleven syllables, the Jagatī twelve and the Gāyatrī only eight, why does the Gāyatrī have this greatness? The answer: it was only through the power of the Gāyatrī that the Triṣṭup and the Jagatī came to have more syllables. This was shown above by citing passages of the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa. That the pervasion of all the savanas also came to the Gāyatrī through that distinction is shown in the Śatapatha too, as follows. Since the account differs somewhat in order, these passages are also cited.

चतुरक्षराणि ह वा आग्रे छंदाग्स्यासुः । ततो जगती सोममच्छापतत्सा श्रीण्यक्षराणि हित्वाजगाम ततस्त्रिष्टुप्सोममच्छापतत्सैकमक्षरग्ं हित्वाजगाम ततो गायत्री सोममच्छापतत्सैतानि चाक्षराणि हरदित्यागच्छत्सोमं च ततोऽष्टाक्षरा गायत्र्यभवत्तस्मादाहुरष्टाक्षरा गायत्री । (श. ब्रा. ४-३-२-७) पूर्वदल्लि छंदस्सुगळिगॆल्ला नाल्कु अक्षरगळु मात्रविद्दवु. सोमाहरणक्कागि जगतियु हारिदाग बळलि मूरु अक्षरगळन्नु दारियल्लि बिट्टु ऒंदक्षरदॊंदिगॆ मात्र हिंतिरुगितु. नंतर त्रिष्टुप्पु हारि ऒंदक्षरवन्नु बिट्टु हिंतुरिगितु. गायत्रियु स्वशक्तियिंद सोमवन्नु तरुवुदर जॊतॆगॆ अल्लि बिट्टु बंदिद्द नाल्कक्षरगळन्नू हिंदक्कॆ तंदितु. आदुदरिंद गायत्रियु अष्टाक्षरात्मक वागि अष्टाक्षरा गायत्री (*caturakṣarāṇi ha vā āgre chaṃdāgsyāsuḥ | tato jagatī somamacchāpatatsā śrīṇyakṣarāṇi hitvājagāma tatastriṣṭupsomamacchāpatatsaikamakṣaragṃ hitvājagāma tato gāyatrī somamacchāpatatsaitāni cākṣarāṇi haradityāgacchatsomaṃ ca tato 'ṣṭākṣarā gāyatryabhavattasmādāhuraṣṭākṣarā gāyatrī | (śa. brā. 4-3-2-7) pūrvadalli chaṃdassugaḷigèllā nālku akṣaragaḷu mātraviddavu. somāharaṇakkāgi jagatiyu hāridāga baḷali mūru akṣaragaḷannu dāriyalli biṭṭu òṃdakṣaradòṃdigè mātra hiṃtirugitu. naṃtara triṣṭuppu hāri òṃdakṣaravannu biṭṭu hiṃturigitu. gāyatriyu svaśaktiyiṃda somavannu taruvudara jòtègè alli biṭṭu baṃdidda nālkakṣaragaḷannū hiṃdakkè taṃditu. ādudariṃda gāyatriyu aṣṭākṣarātmaka vāgi aṣṭākṣarā gāyatrī*) (Śa. Brā. 4-3-2-7)

In the beginning all the metres had only four syllables. When the Jagatī flew to fetch the Soma, it grew tired, left three syllables on the way, and returned with only one. Then the Triṣṭup flew, left one syllable, and returned. The Gāyatrī, by its own power, brought the Soma and also brought back the four syllables left behind there. Therefore the Gāyatrī, being of eight syllables, became famous as "the eight-syllabled Gāyatrī".

तया प्रातःसवनमतन्वत । तस्माद्गायत्रं प्रातःसवनमतन्वत ताग्ंह त्रिष्टुबुवाचोप त्वाहमायानि त्रिभिरक्षरैरुप मा ह्वयस्व मा मा यज्ञादंतर्गा इति तथेति तामुपाह्वयत तत एकादशाक्षरा त्रिष्टुबभवत्तस्मादाहुस्त्रैष्णुभं माध्यंदिनग्ं सवनमिति ॥ (*tayā prātaḥsavanamatanvata | tasmādgāyatraṃ prātaḥsavanamatanvata tāgṃha triṣṭubuvācopa tvāhamāyāni tribhirakṣarairupa mā hvayasva mā mā yajñādaṃtargā iti tatheti tāmupāhvayata tata ekādaśākṣarā triṣṭubabhavattasmādāhustraiṣṇubhaṃ mādhyaṃdinagṃ savanamiti ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 4-3-2-8)

They performed the Prātaḥsavana with the Gāyatrī of such distinction. Therefore the Prātaḥsavana belongs to the Gāyatrī. With the help of the same Gāyatrī they began to perform the Mādhyandinasavana also. Then the Triṣṭup came and begged the Gāyatrī: "I too shall take part with the three syllables left to me; do not leave me without a share in the sacrifice." The Gāyatrī agreed and gave it room too. Therefore the Triṣṭup metre, united with the Gāyatrī, came to have eleven syllables.

### Printed p. 588

तय्यैव तृतीयसवनमतन्वत । ताग्ं ह जगत्युवाचोप त्वाहमायान्येकेनाक्षरेणोप मा ह्वयस्व मा मा यज्ञादंतर्गा इति तथेति तामुपाह्वयत ततो द्वादशाक्षरा जगत्यभवत्तस्मादाहुर्जागतं तृतीयसवनमिति । (*tayyaiva tṛtīyasavanamatanvata | tāgṃ ha jagatyuvācopa tvāhamāyānyekenākṣareṇopa mā hvayasva mā mā yajñādaṃtargā iti tatheti tāmupāhvayata tato dvādaśākṣarā jagatyabhavattasmādāhurjāgataṃ tṛtīyasavanamiti |*) (Śa. Brā. 4-3-2-9)

With the same Gāyatrī they began to perform the Tṛtīyasavana also. Then the Jagatī approached the Gāyatrī and said: "Do not leave me without a share in the sacrifice. I too shall join you with my one remaining syllable." The Gāyatrī agreed. The Jagatī, joined with the eight syllables of the Gāyatrī and again with those three syllables with which the Gāyatrī had joined the Triṣṭup, came to have twelve syllables. Therefore the Tṛtīyasavana is famed as belonging to the Jagatī.

तदाहुः । गायत्राणि वै सर्वाणि सवनानि गायत्रि ह्येवैतदुपस्पजमानैदिति तस्मात्सग्ंसिद्धं प्रातःसवने प्रतिगृह्णीयात् सग्ंसिद्धा हि गायत्रागच्छत् ॥ (*tadāhuḥ | gāyatrāṇi vai sarvāṇi savanāni gāyatri hyevaitadupaspajamānaiditi tasmātsagṃsiddhaṃ prātaḥsavane pratigṛhṇīyāt sagṃsiddhā hi gāyatrāgacchat ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 4-3-2-10)

Because of this pervasion of all the savanas, all the savanas belong to the Gāyatrī. The sacrificers know that only the Gāyatrī kept growing. Since the Gāyatrī, unlike the other metres, suffered no deficiency and was not incomplete, it is praised, and the mantra signifying its victory must be recited in full. If one such mantra is taken as an example and examined, it becomes clear that it contains both the pre-eminence of the Gāyatrī metre and a prayer addressed to the deity Savitṛ, who is designated a Gandharva.

असौ वा आदित्यो देवः सविता.... ....दिव्यो गंधर्वः केतपूः केतं नः पुनात्वित्यसौ वा आदित्यो दिव्यो गंधर्वः । इमं नो देव सवितर्यज्ञं प्रणयेति । असौ वा आदित्यो देवः सविता यदु वा एष यज्जियं कर्म प्रणयति तदनार्तग्ग् स्वस्तु दृचमश्नुते देवाव्यमिति यो देवानवदित्येतत्सखविदग्ग् सत्राजितं धनजितग्ग् स्वर्जितमिति य एतत्सर्वं विंदादित्ये तदृचेत्यृचा स्तॊमगां समर्धय गायत्रेण रथंतरं बृहद्दायत्रवर्तनीति सामानि स्वाहेति..... ॥ तान्येतान्यष्ट् सावित्राणि । अष्टाक्षरा गायत्री गायत्रोऽग्निर्यावानग्निर्यावत्यस्य मात्रा ॥ (*asau vā ādityo devaḥ savitā.... ....divyo gaṃdharvaḥ ketapūḥ ketaṃ naḥ punātvityasau vā ādityo divyo gaṃdharvaḥ | imaṃ no deva savitaryajñaṃ praṇayeti | asau vā ādityo devaḥ savitā yadu vā eṣa yajjiyaṃ karma praṇayati tadanārtagg svastu dṛcamaśnute devāvyamiti yo devānavadityetatsakhavidagg satrājitaṃ dhanajitagg svarjitamiti ya etatsarvaṃ viṃdāditye tadṛcetyṛcā stòmagāṃ samardhaya gāyatreṇa rathaṃtaraṃ bṛhaddāyatravartanīti sāmāni svāheti..... ‖ tānyetānyaṣṭ sāvitrāṇi | aṣṭākṣarā gāyatrī gāyatro 'gniryāvānagniryāvatyasya mātrā ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 6-3-1-19, 21)

The Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā sentence (11-7), "O god Savitṛ, urge on our sacrifice quickly, so that it is accomplished without obstacle," is to be recited. The god Savitṛ is Āditya. All the sacrificial share belongs to him. The prayer is: "May Savitṛ, the purifier of the mind and the Gandharva of the atmosphere, who is Āditya, cause the sacrifice to be accomplished completely." If the Rathantara sāman is joined with the Gāyatrī metre and the Bṛhat sāman with the Gāyatrī measure, and an efficacious mantra is composed and recited, it always secures prosperity and heaven. The mantras recited in prayer to Savitṛ are eight in number; since the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables, the number of these mantras is also eight. Since Agni, the chief of the whole sacrifice, is Gāyatra, Agni's glory is the glory of the Gāyatrī; thus the primacy of the Gāyatrī at the time of sacrifice is declared.

### Printed p. 589

———

11. How can the Gāyatrī, chief in ritual action, be the means to the knowledge of Brahman? Objection and reply.

To make known the primacy of the Gāyatrī, Śaṅkarācārya said that it plays the chief part by three points, the Gāyatrī being the supreme means of knowing the Supreme Brahman, who is beyond ordinary perception. But here another doubt arises. The scriptural descriptions may be true that the Gāyatrī is the support of all the metres that form part of the sacrifice, and that all other metres grew by resting on it. But there is room for the question: merely because it is chief in the sacrifice, which is predominantly ritual action, how can the Gāyatrī also be a means to knowledge of Brahman? Yet the Śrutis themselves declare that the Gāyatrī is of the nature of Brahman, and that knowledge of Brahman is not possible by any means other than Brahman. All the metres useful to the sacrifice, which reflects the principle of Brahman, are indispensable to it; so what is this greatness of the Gāyatrī alone? The answer is that all the other metres cause only impermanent wealth, whereas the Gāyatrī alone can bestow wealth that is eternal and of the nature of Brahman. The greatness of the Gāyatrī is described in the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa thus: एतद्द वै यजमानस्माध्यात्मानमिति.... (*etadda vai yajamānasmādhyātmānamiti....*). And as to which metre should be resorted to at the time of reciting the Praüga-śastra:

गायत्रं प्रउगं कुर्यादित्याहुस्तेजो वै ब्रह्मवर्चसं गायत्री तेजस्वी ब्रह्मवर्चसी भवतीति । औष्ठिहं प्रउगं कुर्यादित्याहुरायुर्वा उष्णिगायुष्मान्भवतीति । आनुष्टुभं प्रउगं कुर्यादित्याहुः क्षत्रं ना अनुष्टुप्क्षत्रस्याप्ता इति । बार्हतं प्रउगं कुर्यादित्याहुः श्रीर्वै बृहती श्री- मान्यवतीति । पाङ्कं प्रउगं कुर्यादित्याहुरन्नं वै पंक्तिरन्नवान्भवतीति । त्रैष्टुभं प्रउगं कुर्याद्वीर्यं वै त्रिष्टुब्बीर्यवान्भवतीति । जागतं प्रउगं कुर्यादित्याहुर्जागता वै पशवः पशुमान्भवतीति । तदु गायत्रमेव कुर्यादब्रह्म वै गायत्री ब्रह्मैतदहर्ब्रह्मणैव तद्ब्रह्म प्रतिपद्यते ॥ (*gāyatraṃ praugaṃ kuryādityāhustejo vai brahmavarcasaṃ gāyatrī tejasvī brahmavarcasī bhavatīti | auṣṭhihaṃ praugaṃ kuryādityāhurāyurvā uṣṇigāyuṣmānbhavatīti | ānuṣṭubhaṃ praugaṃ kuryādityāhuḥ kṣatraṃ nā anuṣṭupkṣatrasyāptā iti | bārhataṃ praugaṃ kuryādityāhuḥ śrīrvai bṛhatī śrī- mānyavatīti | pāṅkaṃ praugaṃ kuryādityāhurannaṃ vai paṃktirannavānbhavatīti | traiṣṭubhaṃ praugaṃ kuryādvīryaṃ vai triṣṭubbīryavānbhavatīti | jāgataṃ praugaṃ kuryādityāhurjāgatā vai paśavaḥ paśumānbhavatīti | tadu gāyatrameva kuryādabrahma vai gāyatrī brahmaitadaharbrahmaṇaiva tadbrahma pratipadyate ‖*) (Ai. Ā. 1-1-3)

### Printed p. 590

If the Praüga-śastra is in the Gāyatrī metre, which is full of splendour and endowed with brahmavarcas, then the man who performs the sacrifice reciting it also becomes splendid and endowed with brahmavarcas; this is the view of some. Another view is that if the Praüga-śastra made of the Uṣṇik, which is life-giving, is recited, the sacrificer obtains long life. Some say that if it is made of the Anuṣṭup, which is full of vigour, the sacrificer becomes vigorous. Others say that by reciting the Praüga made of the Bṛhatī, which is wealth, the sacrificer becomes endowed with wealth. One tradition says that if it is made of the Paṅkti, which is food, and is recited, the sacrificer becomes possessed of the wealth of food. Another tradition says that the Triṣṭup, which is strength, makes it give strength. Still others hold that if the śastra made of the Jagatī, which is wealth in cattle, is recited, the sacrificer obtains wealth in cattle. But wealth in food and the like is all impermanent riches. It is beyond dispute that the eternal wealth of the knowledge of Brahman is obtained only by reciting the Praüga made of the Gāyatrī, which is of the nature of Brahman. Therefore the conclusion is that the Gāyatrī itself is the direct means to the knowledge of Brahman, and no other metre can be.

तदु माधुच्छंदसं (*tadu mādhucchaṃdasaṃ*). It is said that this Praüga made of the Gāyatrī should be made of Madhucchandas. But what is Madhucchandas here? What is the reason for this name? What is the close connection between the Gāyatrī and Madhucchandas? This will be explained later. As stated in the Aitareya Āraṇyaka, it is recited again in many Śruti passages that the Gāyatrī is of the nature of Brahman and that this is the means to knowledge of Brahman.

12. Since the sacrifice, which consists of ritual action, is itself of the nature of Brahman, the above objection has no room.

Even with these Śruti proofs, another question arises here. If knowledge alone were chief here, and one fixed one's aim on knowledge of Brahman through meditation, samādhi and austerity, then one could say that the Gāyatrī is the chief means to knowledge of Brahman. But the primacy of the Gāyatrī is

### Printed p. 591

only in the sacrifice. The sacrifice is predominantly ritual action. So there is also room for the doubt how the Gāyatrī, which is chief in a sacrifice that is predominantly ritual, can directly lead to knowledge. To obtain the answer to this question and to know the chief part of the Gāyatrī in the search for knowledge, one must examine such matters as: what is the true nature of the sacrifice? What is the aim of the sacrifice? Is there opposition between the principle of Brahman and the principle of the sacrifice? The Saṃhitā and Brāhmaṇa passages that set forth the principle of the sacrifice do not describe the sacrifice merely as a rite yielding worldly fruit. In many places they declare the identity of the sacrifice with Prajāpati, the cause of creation, preservation and dissolution.

संवत्सरो यज्ञः प्रजापति स यावानेव यज्ञो यावत्यस्य मात्रा तावंतमेवैतत्परिगृह्णाति ॥ (*saṃvatsaro yajñaḥ prajāpati sa yāvāneva yajño yāvatyasya mātrā tāvaṃtamevaitatparigṛhṇāti ‖*) (Śa. Brā. 1-2-5-12)

In passages such as this, the identity of Prajāpati with the year, which is of the nature of time, and with the sacrifice in the form of the year, is stated. The construction of such a sacrifice is as follows: तं छंदोभिरभितः परिगृह्य (*taṃ chaṃdobhirabhitaḥ parigṛhya*), that is, one should enclose the sacrificial altar with the metres and establish the fire. In the construction of the sacrifice the metres are the most important of all the materials. This sacrificial altar too is not different from the metres.

तानि वा एतानि सप्तविग्ंशतिर्नक्षत्राणि । छंदाग्ंसि ह त्वेवैषोऽग्निश्चितः । तानि वा एतानि सप्तच्छंदाग्ंसि । (*tāni vā etāni saptavigṃśatirnakṣatrāṇi | chaṃdāgṃsi ha tvevaiṣo 'gniścitaḥ | tāni vā etāni saptacchaṃdāgṃsi |*)

अयं नाव लोक एषोऽग्निश्चितः (*ayaṃ nāva loka eṣo 'gniścitaḥ*)

अंतरिक्षग्ंह त्वैवैषोऽग्निश्चितः । .... .... .... द्यौर्हत्वेवेषोऽग्निश्चितः । .... . .... .... .... आदित्यो ह त्वैवैषोऽग्निश्चितः । (*aṃtarikṣagṃha tvaivaiṣo 'gniścitaḥ | .... .... .... dyaurhatveveṣo 'gniścitaḥ | .... . .... .... .... ādityo ha tvaivaiṣo 'gniścitaḥ |*)

This sacrificial altar is the terrestrial world, this is the atmosphere, this is the heavenly world, this is Āditya. Three hundred and sixty directions and intermediate directions surround Āditya. The three hundred and sixty Yajuṣmatī bricks are the three hundred and sixty rays of Āditya. The Sūdadohas are the special principles lying between the rays of Āditya and the directions; these are the seven metres.

सर्वाणि ह त्त्वेव भूतानि । सर्वे देवा एषोऽग्निश्चित आपो वै सर्वे देवाः सर्वाणि भूतानि ता हैता आप एवैषोऽग्निश्चितस्तस्य नाव्या एव परिश्रितः .... .... आत्मायमेव स योऽयं हिरण्मयःपुरुषः । (*sarvāṇi ha ttveva bhūtāni | sarve devā eṣo 'gniścita āpo vai sarve devāḥ sarvāṇi bhūtāni tā haitā āpa evaiṣo 'gniścitastasya nāvyā eva pariśritaḥ .... .... ātmāyameva sa yo 'yaṃ hiraṇmayaḥpuruṣaḥ |*) (Śa. Brā. 10-5-4-1 to 15)

Just as around Āditya the boats in the form of the three hundred and sixty rays surround him, so around this altar the gods, men and others in the form of the Yajuṣmatīs surround it. The body of this altar is Āditya

### Printed p. 592

…the Golden Person who dwells within the sun. How attractive and how weighty is the nature of this Golden Person! It is said:

तस्यैते प्रतिष्ठे । रुक्ष्मश्च पुष्करसर्णं चापश्चादित्यमंडलं .... .... ताविंद्राग्नी द्वे स्वयमातृण्णे इयं चांतरिक्षं च .... .... विश्वज्योतिष एता देवता अग्निर्वायुरादित्य एता ह्येव देवताः .... .... आत्मा स एषः सर्वासामपां मध्यॆ स एष सर्वैः कामैः संपन्नः .... .... ॥ (*tasyaite pratiṣṭhe | rukṣmaśca puṣkarasarṇaṃ cāpaścādityamaṃḍalaṃ .... .... tāviṃdrāgnī dve svayamātṛṇṇe iyaṃ cāṃtarikṣaṃ ca .... .... viśvajyotiṣa etā devatā agnirvāyurāditya etā hyeva devatāḥ .... .... ātmā sa eṣaḥ sarvāsāmapāṃ madhyè sa eṣa sarvaiḥ kāmaiḥ saṃpannaḥ .... .... ‖*)

The golden vessel and the lotus leaf are the two feet of this Golden Person who dwells within the sun. The two ladles on the sacrificial altar are his arms. These are Candra and Agni.**NOTE**. The bricks in the form of the Viśvajyotis are all the deities. Their number is three, and these three reflect Agni, Vāyu and Āditya. The body of this altar is the end of everything. This Golden Person, who has the form of the altar and dwells within the sun, has obtained all desires, and therefore is free from desire and perfectly content.

Thus this principle of sacrifice teaches the unity of the universe, and that the ground of this unity is the principle called Parabrahman. What the Upaniṣads and the like call Parabrahman, the Saṃhitās and Brāhmaṇas call Prajāpati; and they speak of the identity of sacrifice and Prajāpati. The creation of the universe is the fruit of Prajāpati's sacrificial austerity. Prajāpati, the cause of the world, existing before creation and without a second, had to offer himself as the oblation if he was to perform the sacrifice that is the means of creation. By such statements as य आत्मदा बलदा (*ya ātmadā baladā*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-121-2) it is described how Prajāpati carried out creation, whose command all the gods and others obey, and whose shadows are death and immortality. The supreme purpose of the sacrifice is thus declared: that we too should worship that Prajāpati, the cause of the universe, by performing sacrificial rites.

The faith to be placed in the principle of sacrifice is not blind faith. This faith must have the power to grasp the spiritual principle. It shows the relation between the sacrifice, the navel of the world, and the principle of Brahman. The sacrificer whose faith rests on spiritual knowledge recognises the identity between himself and the sacrifice. He knows that all the worldly activity of Parabrahman in the form of Prajāpati is contained in this principle of sacrifice, and that he too takes a share in that wheel of the universe. For this realisation meditation and the vision of the inner eye are absolutely necessary:

पश्यन् मन्ये मनसा चक्षसा तान् य इमं यज्ञमयजंत पूर्वे ॥ (*paśyan manye manasā cakṣasā tān ya imaṃ yajñamayajaṃta pūrve ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-130-6)

### Printed p. 593

"With the help of the inner eye in the form of meditation I know and praise the gods and seers who knew the principle of sacrifice, the root of this worldly activity." Thus the necessity of meditation is shown.

This purpose of sacrifice is declared in the sūkta addressed to the deity Savitṛ, in which one prays: whose Bhargas we desire to know, whose nature as the great light we wish to know, "grant us the meditative intellect" — धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात् (*dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt*).

युंजते मन उत युंजते धियो विप्रा विप्रस्य बृहतो विपश्चितः । वि होत्रा दधे वयुनाविदेक इन्मही देवस्य सवितुः परिष्टुतिः ॥ (*yuṃjate mana uta yuṃjate dhiyo viprā viprasya bṛhato vipaścitaḥ | vi hotrā dadhe vayunāvideka inmahī devasya savituḥ pariṣṭutiḥ ‖*) (Ma. Saṃ. 5-81-1)**NOTE**

This shows the necessity of meditation: the learned priests engaged in sacrificial work concentrate their minds and worship Savitṛ by meditation in the form of yoga. Knowing the divine nature of Savitṛ through this meditation is thus the supreme purpose of the sacrifice. In the present mantra तत्सवितुः (*tatsavituḥ*) the importance of the prayer "grant the dhī" is explained, and this matter will be explained again when the right meaning of the word dhī is examined.

Just as the principle of sacrifice is described as the thread of the universe by such statements as यो यज्ञो विश्वतस्तंतुभिस्तत एकशतं (*yo yajño viśvatastaṃtubhistata ekaśataṃ*), so too the Gāyatrī holds a primary place in carrying out sacrifice. By गायत्री वा इदं सर्वं भूतं यदिदं किंच (*gāyatrī vā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ yadidaṃ kiṃca*), that all beings, moving and unmoving, are of the nature of Gāyatrī, the universal pervasion of Gāyatrī and its having merged the whole world into itself is shown.

**13. Discussion whether Gāyatrī is merely a means to the knowledge of Brahman or the attainable object in the form of knowledge.**

Now, the distinctive character of Gāyatrī as a metre is described in अथातः शिरः । तद्गायत्रीषु भवत्यग्रं वै छंदसां गायत्री । (*athātaḥ śiraḥ | tadgāyatrīṣu bhavatyagraṃ vai chaṃdasāṃ gāyatrī |*) (Ai. Ā. 1-4-1) and so on. For carrying out sacrifices and the like, too, Gāyatrī in the form of a metre holds a most useful primacy. A metre can only be a means for the search after the principle; it cannot itself be the object sought. The doubt therefore arises whether Gāyatrī, which has the form of a metre, can be of the nature of the principle that reflects and teaches the Parabrahman principle, and whether that is possible.

### Printed p. 594

Such a doubt is anticipated in the Brahma-sūtra as well; an answer is given to it and the conclusion is upheld that Gāyatrī is the Parabrahman principle itself and not something different. Since that discussion also establishes the principle by taking Vedic sentences as authority, it may be examined here too.

अपि यदुक्तं पूर्वस्मिन्नपि वाक्ये न ब्रह्म अभिहितमस्ति । गायत्री वा इदं सर्वं भूतं यदिदं किंच, इति गायत्राख्यस्य छंदसोऽभिहित्वात् इति तत् परिहर्तव्यं । कथं पुनः छंदोऽभिधानात् न ब्रह्म अभिहितं इति शक्यते वक्तुं । यावता तावानस्य महिमा इत्येतस्यां ऋचि चतुष्पाद् ब्रह्म दर्शित्वं । नैतदस्ति । गायत्री वा इदं सर्वं इति गायत्रीं उपक्रम्य तामेव भूतपृथिवीशरीरहृदयवाक्प्रभेदैर्वाख्याय । सैषा चतुःप्पदा षड्विधा गायत्री तदेतदृचाभ्यनूक्तं तावानस्य महिमा इति तस्यामेव व्याख्यातरूपायां गायत्रां उदाहृतो मंत्रः कथं अकस्मात् ब्रह्म चतुष्पात् अभिदध्यात् । योऽपि यद्वैतद्ब्रह्मा इति ब्रह्मशब्दः सोऽपि छंदसः प्रकृतत्वात् छंदोविषय एव .... .... तस्मात् छंदोऽभिधानात् न ब्रह्मणः प्रकृतत्वं ॥ (*api yaduktaṃ pūrvasminnapi vākye na brahma abhihitamasti | gāyatrī vā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ yadidaṃ kiṃca, iti gāyatrākhyasya chaṃdaso 'bhihitvāt iti tat parihartavyaṃ | kathaṃ punaḥ chaṃdo 'bhidhānāt na brahma abhihitaṃ iti śakyate vaktuṃ | yāvatā tāvānasya mahimā ityetasyāṃ ṛci catuṣpād brahma darśitvaṃ | naitadasti | gāyatrī vā idaṃ sarvaṃ iti gāyatrīṃ upakramya tāmeva bhūtapṛthivīśarīrahṛdayavākprabhedairvākhyāya | saiṣā catuḥppadā ṣaḍvidhā gāyatrī tadetadṛcābhyanūktaṃ tāvānasya mahimā iti tasyāmeva vyākhyātarūpāyāṃ gāyatrāṃ udāhṛto maṃtraḥ kathaṃ akasmāt brahma catuṣpāt abhidadhyāt | yo 'pi yadvaitadbrahmā iti brahmaśabdaḥ so 'pi chaṃdasaḥ prakṛtatvāt chaṃdoviṣaya eva .... .... tasmāt chaṃdo 'bhidhānāt na brahmaṇaḥ prakṛtatvaṃ ‖*) (Brahma-sūtra, Śā. Bhā. 1-1-25)**NOTE**

Everything in the world, all beings movable and immovable, is Gāyatrī (Chā. U. 3-12-1); the objector's view is that in describing the nature of Gāyatrī this speaks only of the Gāyatrī in the form of a metre and not of a principle pointing to Parabrahman. To refute this, the siddhāntin points out that in the same Chāndogya Upaniṣad the mantra एतावानस्य महिमा (*etāvānasya mahimā*) ("such is its greatness, so boundless") (Chā. U. 3-12-6) declares the nature of Brahman with four feet. Therefore the word Gāyatrī here means the Parabrahman thing, not merely Gāyatrī as a metre. Against this the objector devises another meaning and explains that sentence thus: having begun with गायत्रि वा इदं सर्वं भूतं (*gāyatri vā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ*), the text divides that same Gāyatrī into intermediate divisions — beings, earth, body, heart, speech, breath — saying that it has four feet and is of six kinds; and this is what the Ṛk-mantra describes as एतावानस्य महिमा (*etāvānasya mahimā*). How can such a description of a metre point to Brahman with four feet? Since the metre alone is the topic in hand, the matter of the metre is what is spoken; there is no mention of Parabrahman. So the objector defends his view. The siddhāntin's answer runs as follows:

### Printed p. 595

नैष दोषः । तथा चेतोऽर्पणनिगदात् । तथा गायत्राख्यच्छंदोद्वारेण तदनुगते ब्रह्मणि चेतसः अर्पणं चित्तसमाधानं अनेन ब्राह्मणवाक्येन निगद्यते । गायत्रि वा इदं सर्वं इति । न हि अक्षरसंनिवेशमात्राया गायत्राः सर्वात्मकत्वं संभवति । तस्मात् यत् गायत्राख्यविकारे अनुगतं जगत्कारणं ब्रह्म तदिह सर्वं इत्युच्यते ... .... तस्मात् अस्ति छंदोऽभिधानेऽपि पूर्वस्मिन् वाक्ये चतुष्पात् ब्रह्म निर्दिष्टं । तदेव ज्योतिर्वाक्येऽपि परामृश्यते उपासनानंतरविधानाय ॥ (*naiṣa doṣaḥ | tathā ceto 'rpaṇanigadāt | tathā gāyatrākhyacchaṃdodvāreṇa tadanugate brahmaṇi cetasaḥ arpaṇaṃ cittasamādhānaṃ anena brāhmaṇavākyena nigadyate | gāyatri vā idaṃ sarvaṃ iti | na hi akṣarasaṃniveśamātrāyā gāyatrāḥ sarvātmakatvaṃ saṃbhavati | tasmāt yat gāyatrākhyavikāre anugataṃ jagatkāraṇaṃ brahma tadiha sarvaṃ ityucyate ... .... tasmāt asti chaṃdo 'bhidhāne 'pi pūrvasmin vākye catuṣpāt brahma nirdiṣṭaṃ | tadeva jyotirvākye 'pi parāmṛśyate upāsanānaṃtaravidhānāya ‖*) (Śa. Bhā. Bra. Sū. 1-1.-5)**NOTE**

The objector's view is not consistent. For in the present context it is said that one should place the mind on the supreme thing and meditate; so, through the metre called Gāyatrī, the mind is to be placed on the Brahman that pervades it, and this is said by the mantra sentence गायत्रि वा इदं सर्वं (*gāyatri vā idaṃ sarvaṃ*).**NOTE**. To say that Gāyatrī, which is merely an arrangement of syllables and has the form of a metre, is of the nature of everything would be inconsistent. Therefore it can be said decisively that the thing indicated is Parabrahman itself, existing in the form of the effect called Gāyatrī and being the cause of the whole world. That the cause is not different from the effect is said in the sūtra तदनन्यत्वमारंभणशब्दादिभ्यः (*tadananyatvamāraṃbhaṇaśabdādibhyaḥ*) (2-1-14).

In other Śrutis too it is said that the Parabrahman principle, the cause, should be worshipped through the effect**NOTE**. (Ai. Ā. 3-2-3)

सर्वेषु भूतेष्वेतमेव ब्रह्मेत्याचक्षते ! स एष संवत्सरसमानश्च क्षुर्मयः शोत्रमयश्चंदोमयो मनोमयो वाङ्मय आत्मा स य एवमेतं .... .... .... शंसति ॥ (*sarveṣu bhūteṣvetameva brahmetyācakṣate ! sa eṣa saṃvatsarasamānaśca kṣurmayaḥ śotramayaścaṃdomayo manomayo vāṅmaya ātmā sa ya evametaṃ .... .... .... śaṃsati ‖*) (Ai. Ā. 3-2-3)**NOTE**

The cause-thing that has transformed itself into many forms as effects — eye, ear, metre and so on — is Parabrahman. These Śruti sentences teach the above meaning: that this very Parabrahman thing is to be worshipped in forms such as the metre.

Therefore, although in some places the word Gāyatrī clearly gives the meaning "metre", there is no doubt that the Upaniṣad sentence गायत्री वा इदग्ं सर्वं (*gāyatrī vā idagṃ sarvaṃ*) points to the Parabrahman thing itself. Even though it is counted as a metre, just as Parabrahman, who is supernatural, beyond ordinary worldly perception and the cause, reveals himself through worldly effect-things, so the Gāyatrī principle is described as the Parabrahman principle: सैषा चतुष्पदा गायत्री (*saiṣā catuṣpadā gāyatrī*) (Chā. U. 3-12-5)

### Printed p. 596

Of these four feet, the first three reflect the world in the form of the effect, and the fourth (turīya) foot reflects the Brahman principle in the form of the cause. Even when the word Gāyatrī is taken to mean a metre, its purport must be stated as a metre that possesses both these forms. The first three feet are graspable by worldly understanding; the fourth foot is to be realised through yoga and meditation.

**14. The spiritual character of metre, and the primacy of Gāyatrī in the search for knowledge.**

देवा वै मृत्योर्भिभ्यतस्त्रयीं विद्यां प्राविशंस्ते छंदोभिराच्छादयन्यदेभिराच्छादयन्स्छंदसां छंदस्त्वं । (*devā vai mṛtyorbhibhyatastrayīṃ vidyāṃ prāviśaṃste chaṃdobhirācchādayanyadebhirācchādayanschaṃdasāṃ chaṃdastvaṃ |*) (Bhā. U. 1-4-2)**NOTE**

This sentence states the general characteristic of metre. When the gods, afraid of death, entered the threefold knowledge (trayī), the threefold knowledge concealed them with the metres. The word chandas is derived from the root chad, meaning "cover, conceal". Because they covered them from death, they are called chandas; thus its characteristic is stated. (The root is also used in the sense "to gladden".)

However, even though the metres concealed the gods from the face of death, death discovered that these gods were hidden in the trayī; thus a shortcoming in the power of the metres is also shown. The purport is that in such contexts the metre is worldly and belongs to the world of effects. Although such a metre gives joy, that joy is limited. In speaking of the Gāyatrī metre too, both these forms are described and Gāyatrī is praised. The Upaniṣads praise Gāyatrī by saying that its first three feet reflect the lower principle and the fourth foot reflects the higher principle.

भूमिरंतरिक्षं द्यौरित्यष्टावक्षराणि । अष्टाक्षरं ह वा एकं गायत्रै पदं । एतदु हैवास्या एतदेवं पदं वेद । (*bhūmiraṃtarikṣaṃ dyaurityaṣṭāvakṣarāṇi | aṣṭākṣaraṃ ha vā ekaṃ gāyatrai padaṃ | etadu haivāsyā etadevaṃ padaṃ veda |*) (Bṛ. U. 5-14-1)

Earth, atmosphere, heaven: these eight syllables are the first foot of Gāyatrī. Thus these three worlds together become one foot of Gāyatrī. One who knows this principle obtains the wealth of these three worlds.

### Printed p. 597

यजो यजूग्ंषि, सामानि इत्यष्टावक्षराणि । अष्टाक्षरं ह ना एकं गायत्रै पदं । एतदु हैवास्या एतत् । स यावतीयं त्रयी विद्या तावद्ध जयति योऽस्या एतदेवं पदं वेद । (*yajo yajūgṃṣi, sāmāni ityaṣṭāvakṣarāṇi | aṣṭākṣaraṃ ha nā ekaṃ gāyatrai padaṃ | etadu haivāsyā etat | sa yāvatīyaṃ trayī vidyā tāvaddha jayati yo 'syā etadevaṃ padaṃ veda |*) (Bṛ. U. 5-14-2)

Ṛcs, Yajus formulas, Sāmans: these eight syllables are the second foot of Gāyatrī. One who knows this principle obtains all the wealth of knowledge to be gained from the trayī, the treasury of knowledge.

प्राणोऽपानो व्यान इत्याष्टावक्षराणि । अष्टाक्षरं ह वा एकं गायत्रैशि पदं । एतदु हैवास्या एतत् । स यावदिदं प्राणि तावद्ध जयति योऽस्या एतदेवं पदं वेद । (*prāṇo 'pāno vyāna ityāṣṭāvakṣarāṇi | aṣṭākṣaraṃ ha vā ekaṃ gāyatraiśi padaṃ | etadu haivāsyā etat | sa yāvadidaṃ prāṇi tāvaddha jayati yo 'syā etadevaṃ padaṃ veda |*) (Bṛ. U. 5-4-3)**NOTE**

The three principles prāṇa, apāna and vyāna are the third foot of Gāyatrī, which consists of eight syllables. One who knows this principle obtains all the wealth of power of the whole class of living beings. The sun, shining with his own radiance and visible to the whole world, is the fourth foot of Gāyatrī. Although he has a nature beyond worldly perception, the sun takes a form open to perception and appears to all; hence the epithet दर्शतं (*darśataṃ*) here. Because he shines in the excellent atmosphere, surpassing all the worlds full of darkness, there is the epithet परोरजाः (*parorajāḥ*). One who knows the nature of this fourth foot becomes radiant and endowed with Brahmanic splendour.

सैषा गायत्र्येतस्मिंस्तुरीये दर्शते पदे परोरजसि प्रतिष्ठिता । तद्वै तत्सत्ये प्रतिष्ठितं । चक्षुर्वै सत्यं । चक्षुर्हि वै सत्यं .... .... तस्मादाहुर्बलं सत्यादोगीय इति । एवं वैषा गायत्र्यध्यात्मं प्रतिष्ठिता । सा हैषा गयांस्तत्रे । प्राणा वै गयाः तत्पाणांस्तत्रे तद्यद्धयांस्तत्रे तस्माद्दायत्री नाम । स यामेवामुं सावित्रिमन्वाह । एवैष सा । स यस्मा अन्वाह तस्य प्राणास्त्रायंते ॥ (*saiṣā gāyatryetasmiṃsturīye darśate pade parorajasi pratiṣṭhitā | tadvai tatsatye pratiṣṭhitaṃ | cakṣurvai satyaṃ | cakṣurhi vai satyaṃ .... .... tasmādāhurbalaṃ satyādogīya iti | evaṃ vaiṣā gāyatryadhyātmaṃ pratiṣṭhitā | sā haiṣā gayāṃstatre | prāṇā vai gayāḥ tatpāṇāṃstatre tadyaddhayāṃstatre tasmāddāyatrī nāma | sa yāmevāmuṃ sāvitrimanvāha | evaiṣa sā | sa yasmā anvāha tasya prāṇāstrāyaṃte ‖*)

On this fourth (turīya) foot, described as parorajas and darśata, Gāyatrī is established. That is the world of truth. Therefore Gāyatrī is established on truth. The eye is truth. How? When one man says "I saw" and another says "I heard" and they dispute, the word of the one who saw carries greater authority.

### Printed p. 598

That truth rests on strength. Strength is the vital breath (prāṇa). Therefore those who know say that strength has more substance than truth. The senses of the body are the *gayas*. The breath guards these *gayas*, and for that reason the name is Gāyatrī. This Gāyatrī is itself present in the body in the form of the chief vital breath. It is also called Sāvitrī, the verse the teacher gives to the pupil as instruction. It guards the vital breaths of whoever receives this instruction.

तां हैतमेके सावित्रिमनुष्टुभमन्वाहुः । वागनुष्टुप् । तद्वाचमनुब्रूम इति । न तथा कुर्यात् । गायत्रीमेव सावित्रिमनुब्रूयात् । यदि ह वा अप्येवंविद्बह्विव प्रतिगृह्णाति न हैव तद्दायत्रा एकंचन पदं प्रति । (*tāṃ haitameke sāvitrimanuṣṭubhamanvāhuḥ | vāganuṣṭup | tadvācamanubrūma iti | na tathā kuryāt | gāyatrīmeva sāvitrimanubrūyāt | yadi ha vā apyevaṃvidbahviva pratigṛhṇāti na haiva taddāyatrā ekaṃcana padaṃ prati |*) (Chā. U. 5-14-5)

Speech (vāc) is in the form of the Anuṣṭubh, and speech is also of the form of the Gāyatrī. For this reason some teachers instruct the Sāvitrī in the form of the Anuṣṭubh. That is not right. Only the Sāvitrī in the form of the Gāyatrī should be taught. A man who knows this truth may accept a very abundant gift, and yet it does not equal even one foot of the Gāyatrī.

स य इमांस्त्रीन्‌लोकान्पूर्णान् प्रतिगृह्णीयात्, सोऽस्या एतत्पथमं पदमाप्नुयात् । अथ यावतीयं त्रयी विद्या यस्तावत्पतिगृह्णीयात् सोऽस्याएतद्वितीयं पदमाप्नुयात् अथ यावदिदं प्राणि यस्तावत्पतिगृह्णीयात् सोऽस्या एतत्तृतीयं पदमाप्नुयात् अथास्या एतदेव तुरीयं दर्शतं पदं परोरजा य एष तपति । नैव केनच नाप्यं कुत उ एतावत्पतिगृह्णीयात् । (*sa ya imāṃstrīnlokānpūrṇān pratigṛhṇīyāt, so 'syā etatpathamaṃ padamāpnuyāt | atha yāvatīyaṃ trayī vidyā yastāvatpatigṛhṇīyāt so 'syāetadvitīyaṃ padamāpnuyāt atha yāvadidaṃ prāṇi yastāvatpatigṛhṇīyāt so 'syā etattṛtīyaṃ padamāpnuyāt athāsyā etadeva turīyaṃ darśataṃ padaṃ parorajā ya eṣa tapati | naiva kenaca nāpyaṃ kuta u etāvatpatigṛhṇīyāt |*) (Bhā. U. 5-19-6) **NOTE**

One who accepts only these three worlds, full of wealth, obtains only the first foot of the Gāyatrī. One who accepts only the threefold Veda, the treasure of knowledge, obtains the second foot as well. One who accepts only the whole creation of living beings obtains the third foot as his reward. But no wealth in the world can equal the reward that falls to the man who has realised the fourth foot, the visible one, whose nature is "beyond the dust". Therefore the Gāyatrī is to be worshipped in this manner (Śaṅkara's commentary). The meaning is that the full form of the Gāyatrī is to be worshipped in the form of meditation.

एवं हैवैवं विद्यद्यपि बह्विव पापं कुरुते सर्वमेव तत्संप्साय शुद्धः पूतोऽजरोऽमृतः संभवति । (*evaṃ haivaivaṃ vidyadyapi bahviva pāpaṃ kurute sarvameva tatsaṃpsāya śuddhaḥ pūto 'jaro 'mṛtaḥ saṃbhavati |*) (Bhā. U. 5-14-8) **NOTE**

Even if one who knows the principle of the Gāyatrī in full should by chance commit sinful acts, he burns all of them and becomes pure, ageless and immortal. Because Agni is the mouth of the Gāyatrī

### Printed p. 599

तस्या अग्नीरेव मुखं (*tasyā agnīreva mukhaṃ*): the meaning is that one who knows the principle of the Gāyatrī in full obtains the power of Agni, who burns up sins. Thus the full nature of the Gāyatrī, both manifest and unmanifest, is explained in the above sentences of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad. In the Chāndogya Upaniṣad too the all-pervading nature of the Gāyatrī is described in the sentences quoted below.

15. How can a metre with a fixed group of syllables be of the form of the all-pervading Brahman?

गायत्री वा इदं सर्वं भूतं यदिदं किंच वाग्वै गायत्री वाग्वा इदं सर्वं भूतं गायति त्रायते च । (*gāyatrī vā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ yadidaṃ kiṃca vāgvai gāyatrī vāgvā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ gāyati trāyate ca |*) (Chā. U. 3-12-1)

छंदोमात्रायाः सर्वभूतत्वमनुपपन्नं इति गायत्रीकारणं वाचं शब्दरूपमापादयति गायत्री वाग्वै गायत्रीति ॥ (*chaṃdomātrāyāḥ sarvabhūtatvamanupapannaṃ iti gāyatrīkāraṇaṃ vācaṃ śabdarūpamāpādayati gāyatrī vāgvai gāyatrīti ‖*) (Śa. Bhā.) **NOTE**

In describing the all-pervading nature of the Gāyatrī, saying that all beings, sentient and insentient, are the Gāyatrī, the text foresees that a doubt may arise, and so it states the identity of speech with the Gāyatrī: वाग्वै गायत्रि (*vāgvai gāyatri*). A question arises here. The doubt is how a metre that is merely a collection of syllables can be all-pervading and be all beings. The answer is to declare that speech itself is the Gāyatrī. What then is the nature and power of speech? Its power is to illuminate the whole business of the universe completely and to be of the nature of the universe. Since the existence of the whole world is made manifest by it, and since the protection and carrying on of the whole world belong to speech, speech pervades the whole world and is identical with it. That this goddess of speech is called by the name Gāyatrī explains one aspect of the Gāyatrī. Moreover,

या वै सा गायत्रीयं वाव सा येयं पृथिव्यस्यां हीदं सर्वं भूतं प्रतिष्ठितमेतामेव नातिशीयते । (*yā vai sā gāyatrīyaṃ vāva sā yeyaṃ pṛthivyasyāṃ hīdaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ pratiṣṭhitametāmeva nātiśīyate |*) (A. U. 3-17-2) (Chā. U. 3-12-2) **NOTE**

Just as the Gāyatrī was called speech because it sings (gāyati) and protects the existence of all beings, so here the Gāyatrī is called the earth, since it has the nature and power of the earth. All beings rest on the earth and are established here. They do not cross this limit. Therefore the Gāyatrī and the earth are identical.

### Printed p. 600

16. Two ways of worshipping the Gāyatrī.

Identity with the outer world.

A man who worships may worship the Gāyatrī from two points of view. First, through meditation on the Gāyatrī he may know the whole outer world, earth, atmosphere and the rest, and understand that all of it is a particular manifestation of the Gāyatrī's glory. Or, from the spiritual point of view, he may know the particular principles within a man's body, and know that these too are manifestations of the Gāyatrī's glory. The sentences of the Upaniṣad describe this matter also.

या वै सा पृथिवीयं वाव सा यदिदमस्मान्पुरुषे शरीरमस्मिन् हीमे प्राणाः प्रतिष्ठिता एतदेव नातिशीयंते ॥ (*yā vai sā pṛthivīyaṃ vāva sā yadidamasmānpuruṣe śarīramasmin hīme prāṇāḥ pratiṣṭhitā etadeva nātiśīyaṃte ‖*) (Chā. U. 3-12-3)

The principle we call the earth is itself, in the form of the aggregate of effect and cause, the body of the man. Just as all beings are established on the earth, so all the chief vital breaths too are established in this body. Just as all beings stay in their fixed condition without passing beyond the earth, so these chief vital breaths too remain within their fixed limit without passing beyond the order of the body.

यद्वै तत्पुरुषे शरीरमिदं वाव तद्यदिदमस्मिन्नंतः पुरुषे हृदयमस्मिन्हीमे प्राणाः प्रतिष्ठिता एतदेव नातिशीयंते ॥ (*yadvai tatpuruṣe śarīramidaṃ vāva tadyadidamasminnaṃtaḥ puruṣe hṛdayamasminhīme prāṇāḥ pratiṣṭhitā etadeva nātiśīyaṃte ‖*) (Chā. U. 3-12-4)

The bodily principle that we call the Gāyatrī is the lotus of the heart of the man. It is here that the principle of the chief vital breath is established. The principle of breath does not pass beyond this limit.

सैषा चतुष्पदा पद्विधा गायत्री तदेतदृचाभ्यनूक्तं । (*saiṣā catuṣpadā padvidhā gāyatrī tadetadṛcābhyanūktaṃ |*)

This Gāyatrī, which has four feet and is of six kinds, is described in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā in this way:

### Printed p. 601

एतानानस्य महिमातो ज्यायाश्च पूरुषः । पादोऽस्य विश्वा भूतानि त्रिपादस्यामृतं दिवि ॥ (*etānānasya mahimāto jyāyāśca pūruṣaḥ | pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni tripādasyāmṛtaṃ divi ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-3) **NOTE**

This is a description of the greatness of the Supreme Person. "Etāvān" means: all this universe, of the nature of the three times and having the forms of the sentient and the insentient, is the manifestation of this Supreme Person. But the Person's own greatness exceeds all this. The whole universe is only one quarter of this Person. All the remaining parts stay as radiance in his own indestructible, luminous, supra-natural nature.

Description of identity with the inner spiritual principle.

In this description the identity of the Supreme Person with the Gāyatrī is stated. Śrī Śaṅkarācārya explains this:

तावानस्य गायत्राख्यस्य ब्रह्मणः समस्तस्य महिमा विभूतिविस्तारः ॥ (*tāvānasya gāyatrākhyasya brahmaṇaḥ samastasya mahimā vibhūtivistāraḥ ‖*)

He says that the nature and the special glory of the Supreme Brahman, known as the Gāyatrī, are described by these sentences, and he explains the words *pāda* and *tripāt* as set out above.

Although the Upaniṣadic sentences quoted above state the identity of the Gāyatrī with the Supreme Brahman, there are differences in some respects between what is described in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad and what is praised in the Chāndogya. One must first note that difference; then examine which principles of the Supreme Reality the descriptions of the three feet, the fourth foot and so on convey; and, if the deity Savitṛ praised in the present mantra तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं (*tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ*) is itself the Supreme Principle, how these epithets are used in the Saṃhitā and elsewhere.

All beings, the threefold knowledge, the earth, the body, the heart and the chief vital breath are one foot of the Gāyatrī whose nature is the Supreme Reality, or of the Supreme Reality whose nature is the Gāyatrī. This foot is *mūrta*, that is, perceptible to ordinary worldly perception. According to the Chāndogya description, the other three feet also have an ageless, supra-natural form, situated in the atmosphere, as is said in त्रिपादूर्ध्वमुदैत् (*tripādūrdhvamudait*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-3). The explanation of the Bṛhadāraṇyaka is somewhat different. The first three feet are of the nature of the three worlds, of the form of speech beginning with the Ṛk, and of the form of prāṇa, apāna and vyāna. These have a concrete (*mūrta*) form. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka description is that the fourth (turīya) foot lies beyond ordinary perception, is situated in the atmosphere and is contained within the sun

### Printed p. 602

. In these two explanations there is not much difference in principle. Therefore it cannot be said that one contradicts the other. In the present context one must examine how other Śruti passages describe the nature of the fourth foot of the Brahman whose nature is the Gāyatrī.

17. The nature of the three feet and the fourth foot of the Gāyatrī.

The meaning of the explanation "pādo 'sya viśvā bhūtāni".

In the Māṇḍūkya-kārikā and in the other commentaries connected with it, the word *turīya* has a technical sense. In the description of the spiritual nature of the principle, when the states of a person such as waking are explained,

सर्वग्न् हैतद्ब्रह्मायमात्मा ब्रह्म सोऽयमात्मा चतुष्पात् । (*sarvagn haitadbrahmāyamātmā brahma so 'yamātmā catuṣpāt |*) (Mā. U. 2) **NOTE**

After stating the identity of the Self with Brahman, the text declares the four states of the Brahman-substance consisting of four feet, or of the Self in the form of Brahman. This Self, who is both the Supreme Brahman and the lower Brahman, denoted by Oṃkāra, has four feet. Their nature is as follows:

(1) जागरितस्थानो बहिष्प्रज्ञः (*jāgaritasthāno bahiṣprajñaḥ*): one whose place is the waking state and whose consciousness is directed outward.

(2) स्वप्नस्थानोऽंतःप्रज्ञः (*svapnasthāno 'ṃtaḥprajñaḥ*): one whose place is the dream state, the inwardly conscious one.

(3) सुषुप्तस्थान एकीभूतः (*suṣuptasthāna ekībhūtaḥ*): the knower (prājña) in the state of deep sleep, dense with knowledge, who sees not even a dream.

(4) नांतःप्रज्ञं न बहिष्प्रज्ञं नोभयतः प्रज्ञं .... .... अदृष्टमव्यवहार्यं .... .... शांतं शिवमदैतं चतुर्थं मन्यंते स आत्मा स विज्ञेयः ॥ (*nāṃtaḥprajñaṃ na bahiṣprajñaṃ nobhayataḥ prajñaṃ .... .... adṛṣṭamavyavahāryaṃ .... .... śāṃtaṃ śivamadaitaṃ caturthaṃ manyaṃte sa ātmā sa vijñeyaḥ ‖*)

The Self who is neither inwardly conscious nor outwardly conscious, who does not fall within ordinary perception, who is peaceful, auspicious, the essence of the one Self-awareness, of non-dual nature, is the Turīya. The meaning is that he transcends the three feet commonly perceived by the world and has a fourth nature. The same Self is praised as एष त आत्मांतराम्यमृतोऽदृष्टो द्रष्टा (*eṣa ta ātmāṃtarāmyamṛto 'dṛṣṭo draṣṭā*)

### Printed p. 603

श्रुतः श्रोता (*śrutaḥ śrotā*) (Bṛ. U. 3-7-23): he is the witness of the whole world but is not visible to the world's sight; he hears everything but does not fall within the world's hearing; and so on. The Turīya state, described as having a fourth foot that transcends the three feet of the world, is well known in the world of philosophical systems (darśana). The same meaning must be stated here too, in describing the nature of the Supreme Brahman whose nature is the Gāyatrī. When describing a particular principle that is supra-natural and beyond the world, the word *turīya* is seen to be used in the same sense in the Ṛk-Saṃhitā too. For example:

एष स्य भानुरुदियर्ति युज्यते रथः परिज्मा दिवो अस्य सानवि । पृक्षासो आस्मिन्मिथुना अधि त्रयो दृतिस्तुरीयो मधुनो वि रिष्यते ॥ (*eṣa sya bhānurudiyarti yujyate rathaḥ parijmā divo asya sānavi | pṛkṣāso āsminmithunā adhi trayo dṛtisturīyo madhuno vi riṣyate ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 4-45-1)

This is a description of the course of the sun. It says that the three kinds of food, visible and well known on his chariot, shine, and also the fourth (turīya) food, supra-natural and sweeter than these (known as *madhu* in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka and other texts). Although this fourth food in the form of honey shines with its own radiance, it differs in principle from the first three foods. The meaning is that, just as the radiance of the golden Person within the sun has a splendour greater than the mere radiance of the sun, so the radiance of this food, of the nature of honey, is worthy of praise.

स्वर्भानोरध यदिंद्र माया अवो दिवो वर्तमाना अवाहन् । गूह्लं सूर्यं तमसापव्रतेन तुरीयेण ब्रह्मणाविंददत्रिः ॥ (*svarbhānoradha yadiṃdra māyā avo divo vartamānā avāhan | gūhlaṃ sūryaṃ tamasāpavratena turīyeṇa brahmaṇāviṃdadatriḥ ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-40-6)

Here it is said that the sage Atri, by four kinds of mantras, destroyed four kinds of darkness and came to know the special powers covered by it. This is a description of the sun's radiance. That is, the sun's form is of one kind from the world's point of view. The radiance that falls on everyone's eye is common to the world. A radiance greater than that is not perceptible to ordinary sight. For it the help of the mantra and a special meditation prompted by it are necessary. In the same way, if the darkness is understood as the ignorance whose form is darkness, or as the darkness whose form is ignorance, then the meaning is clear that the divine radiance of the sun in the Turīya state can be known only through the power of the Turīya mantra. In the same way,

चमूषच्छ्येनः शकुनो विभृत्वा गोविंदुर्द्रप्स आयुधानि बिभ्रत् । अपामूर्मिं सचमानः समुद्रं तुरीयं धाम महिषो विवक्ति ॥ (*camūṣacchyenaḥ śakuno vibhṛtvā goviṃdurdrapsa āyudhāni bibhrat | apāmūrmiṃ sacamānaḥ samudraṃ turīyaṃ dhāma mahiṣo vivakti ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-96-19)

### Printed p. 604
In this mantra there is praise of the world of the Moon. The sense of the mantra is that Soma, who frequents the atmosphere, shone as he resorted to the world of the Moon, which lies even beyond the world of the Sun. This same lunar world is described differently in the Upaniṣads. To show that in the present context it is a supernatural, divine world, Sāyaṇa has explained it as सूरलोकस्योपरि वर्तमाने (*sūralokasyopari vartamāne*). Here too the word तुरीय (*turīya*) points to the divine abode of the Moon and so expresses a special meaning. Thus the word तुरीय (*turīya*) is used in the Ṛksaṃhitā also to denote the supernatural highest reality.

When it is said that this fourth part is beyond the other three parts of the universe, it must not be understood as different from them. The sense is that one single reality pervades the natural universe and is also transcendent to it. How is that? स भूमिं विश्वतो वृत्वात्यतिष्ठद्दशांगुलं (*sa bhūmiṃ viśvato vṛtvātyatiṣṭhaddaśāṃgulaṃ*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-90-1): the one Supreme Person-principle, pervading the universe, stood beyond it by the measure of ten fingers. What "ten fingers" means here will be explained later according to context.

18. The Supreme Person's pervasion of the universe and his transcendence of it.

रूपंरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रतिचक्षणाय । इंद्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (*rūpaṃrūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tadasya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya | iṃdro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hyasya harayaḥ śatā daśa ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-47-18)

In this mantra the pervasion of the universe is clearly stated. It is a well-known mantra, cited in the Upaniṣads and elsewhere. It is addressed to Indra and describes Indra's great glory. The sense is that Indra himself, assuming the forms of many deities such as Agni, Viṣṇu and Rudra, and the forms of all the natural principles in the universe, pervades the universe as one divine principle in the form of the universe. Sāyaṇa takes this mantra as one that teaches a spiritual principle and has explained it as being the description of the nature of the Supreme Brahman. Here "Indra" means the Supreme Self. That Supreme Self, all-pervading like space and of the nature of eternal bliss, being one, enters all the bodies in the universe according to their respective limiting conditions and attains the variety and division called individual selves. He explains that the Supreme Self, to whom pervasion of the universe and a form transcending the universe belong as equal attributes, is described in this way.

अग्निर्यथैको भुवनं प्रविष्टो रूपंरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव । (*agniryathaiko bhuvanaṃ praviṣṭo rūpaṃrūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva |*)
(९ठ ५-९ (*9ṭha 5-9*))**NOTE**

In Upaniṣadic mantras of this kind also the pervasion of the universe is described as stated above. वृक्ष इव स्तब्धो दिव तिष्ठत्येकस्तेनेदं पूर्णं पुरुषेण-सर्वं (*vṛkṣa iva stabdho diva tiṣṭhatyekastenedaṃ pūrṇaṃ puruṣeṇa-sarvaṃ*)**NOTE**: the whole universe is pervaded by the Supreme Person, who, going beyond the limit of the universe and being transcendent to it, stands

### Printed p. 605
immovable, established like a tree. This attribute of pervasion was also described when the nature of the Gāyatrī was described; it was stated above by citing the sentence एतावानस्य महिमातोज्यायांश्च पूरुषः (*etāvānasya mahimātojyāyāṃśca pūruṣaḥ*). The same point is described in the Chāndogya by the sentences cited below.

19. The similarity of outer space and heart-space.

यद्वै तद्ब्रह्मेतिदं नाव तद्योऽयं बहिर्धा पुरुषादाकाशो यो वै स बहिर्धा पुरुषादाकाशः ॥ आयं नाव स योऽयमंतः पुरुष आकाशो यो वै सोऽंतःपुरुष आकाशः अयं नाव स योऽयमंतर्हृदय आकाशस्तदेतत्पूर्णमप्रवृत्तिपूर्णामप्रवर्तिनीं श्रियं लभते य एवं वेद ॥ (*yadvai tadbrahmetidaṃ nāva tadyo 'yaṃ bahirdhā puruṣādākāśo yo vai sa bahirdhā puruṣādākāśaḥ ‖ āyaṃ nāva sa yo 'yamaṃtaḥ puruṣa ākāśo yo vai so 'ṃtaḥpuruṣa ākāśaḥ ayaṃ nāva sa yo 'yamaṃtarhṛdaya ākāśastadetatpūrṇamapravṛttipūrṇāmapravartinīṃ śriyaṃ labhate ya evaṃ veda ‖*)
(Chā. U. 3-12-7 to 9)

This Supreme Brahman, praised in the form of the Gāyatrī and having four quarters, is itself the space that pervades the outer world. This very principle of space, pervading the outer world of the person, is also the person's inner principle. This Brahman-principle called Gāyatrī, in the heart-space, is all-pervading and immovable. One who knows this principle obtains the wealth of knowledge, all-pervading, eternal and steady, and happiness. The nature of this Supreme principle in the lotus of the heart is to be worshipped through meditation.

दह्रं विपापं वरमेऽत्मभूतं यत्पुंडरीकं पुरमध्यसग्‌स्थं । तत्रापि दह्रं गगनं विशोकस्तस्मिन्यदंतस्तदुपासितव्यं ॥ (*dahraṃ vipāpaṃ varame 'tmabhūtaṃ yatpuṃḍarīkaṃ puramadhyasagsthaṃ | tatrāpi dahraṃ gaganaṃ viśokastasminyadaṃtastadupāsitavyaṃ ‖*)
(Tai. U. U. 4-12-3)**NOTE**

The Brahman-principle described in this mantra is described by the Chāndogya sentence अंतर्हृदयाकाशः (*aṃtarhṛdayākāśaḥ*). Since the Gāyatrī too is described in this way by epithets that establish Brahman, the following matters must be examined. What is meant here by heart-space? What is the lotus of the heart? If the principle of space, which is the support of the Gāyatrī that is both within the lotus of the heart and, at that very time, pervades the whole outer universe—earth, atmosphere and the rest—is the Supreme Brahman, what relation is shown between this principle of space and the Vyāhṛtis beginning with भूः (*bhūḥ*), which are limbs of the Gāyatrī? What is the relation between the Praṇava, which has the Vyāhṛtis as its members, and the Brahman that is of the nature of the Gāyatrī? In what way does the Praṇava become the chief means to the realisation of Brahman? Is the Gāyatrī itself of the nature of the Praṇava? and so on.

### Printed p. 606
Sentences such as अंतर्बहिश्च तत्सर्वं व्याप्य नारायणः स्थितः (*aṃtarbahiśca tatsarvaṃ vyāpya nārāyaṇaḥ sthitaḥ*) teach that the outer principle that pervades all the worlds is the same as the principle within the heart of the person. This one principle is denoted by other names such as Brahman, space and Gāyatrī. In the present context, this pervasion of the inside and the outside is stated exactly also when the three forms Brahman, space and Gāyatrī are described, and it is also made plain that all three are other names of one principle.

एषा गायत्र्यध्यात्मं प्रतिष्ठिता सा हैषा गयांस्तत्रे प्राणा वै गयास्तत्पाणांस्तत्रे तद्यद्गयांस्तत्रे तस्माद्गायत्री नाम स यामेवामूं सावित्रिमन्वाहैवैष सा स यस्मा अन्वाह तस्य प्राणांस्त्रायते ॥ (*eṣā gāyatryadhyātmaṃ pratiṣṭhitā sā haiṣā gayāṃstatre prāṇā vai gayāstatpāṇāṃstatre tadyadgayāṃstatre tasmādgāyatrī nāma sa yāmevāmūṃ sāvitrimanvāhaivaiṣa sā sa yasmā anvāha tasya prāṇāṃstrāyate ‖*)
(Bṛ. U. 5-14-4)

As explained in the sentences cited above, the Gāyatrī-principle that is described by epithets such as परोरजाः (*parorajāḥ*) and that pervades the universe is the very one that, in its spiritual form, lies within the heart; thus the pervasion of the Gāyatrī both within and without is taught. In the same way, describing the nature of space:

यावान् ना अयमाकाशस्तानानेषोऽंतर्हृदय आकाश उभे अस्मिन् द्यावापृथिवी अंतरेव समाहिते उभावग्निश्च वायुश्च सूराचंद्रमसावुभौ विद्युन्नक्षत्राणि यच्चास्केहास्ति यच्च नास्ति सर्वं तदस्मिन् समाहितमिति ॥ (*yāvān nā ayamākāśastānāneṣo 'ṃtarhṛdaya ākāśa ubhe asmin dyāvāpṛthivī aṃtareva samāhite ubhāvagniśca vāyuśca sūrācaṃdramasāvubhau vidyunnakṣatrāṇi yaccāskehāsti yacca nāsti sarvaṃ tadasmin samāhitamiti ‖*)
(Bhā. U. 8-1-3)**NOTE**

In this Brahman-city, the body, there is a subtle house in the form of a lotus. That is the heart-space. It is the dwelling-place of Brahman. One must search for it and see the Brahman-principle there: यदिदमस्मिन् ब्रह्मपुरे दहरं पुंडरीकं वेश्य दहरोऽस्मिन्नंतराकाशस्तस्मिन्यदंतस्तदन्वेष्टव्यं तद्वाव विजिज्ञासितव्यमिति (*yadidamasmin brahmapure daharaṃ puṃḍarīkaṃ veśya daharo 'sminnaṃtarākāśastasminyadaṃtastadanveṣṭavyaṃ tadvāva vijijñāsitavyamiti*) (Chā. U. 8-1-1). The nature of this subtle inner space, which contains the Brahman-principle that is greater than the cosmic egg, is this: as widely as the outer space spreads, so widely does this heart-space spread. In it both heaven and earth are spread; moreover, wind and fire, moon and sun, lightning and stars, whatever is contained within the body and whatever is not—all is contained in this small space. This heart-space is extremely subtle and free from sin. It is the best dwelling-place. In the form of a lotus, in the middle of the city that is the body, in this subtle heart there is a space still subtler, and the Brahman-principle that is contained in that space is to be worshipped: thus the heart-space is described.

### Printed p. 607
20. The Gāyatrī in the form of speech, and the space that is the source of name-and-form usage.

वाग्वै गायत्री । (*vāgvai gāyatrī |*) वाग्वा इदं सर्वं भूतं गायति त्रायते च । (*vāgvā idaṃ sarvaṃ bhūtaṃ gāyati trāyate ca |*) Because the existence of the whole world is revealed only by speech, and because the protection and maintenance of the whole world belongs to speech, speech itself pervades the whole world and is identical with it. It was stated above that this goddess of speech is called by the name Gāyatrī. In many places it is stated that there is a relation of support and supported between the heart-space explained here and speech, which is of the nature of the Word-Brahman and is denoted by the name Gāyatrī, and therefore also that the two are one. Stating the same relation in the Chāndogya also, it says that space is the support of speech, which is the source of all worldly usage.

आकाशो वै नाम नामरूपयोर्निर्वहिता ते यदंतरा तद्ब्रह्म तदमृतं स आत्मा । (*ākāśo vai nāma nāmarūpayornirvahitā te yadaṃtarā tadbrahma tadamṛtaṃ sa ātmā |*)
(Chā. U. 8-14-1)

Space itself is the cause of the individual division called name and form. He who is within it is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Self. Śrī Śaṅkarācārya quoted this sentence in the section on the Daharādhikaraṇa in his Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya and declared the identity of the Supreme Brahman with this small space.

प्रसिद्धेश्व—इतश्च परमेश्वर एव दहरोऽस्मिन्नंतराकाश इत्युच्यते । (*prasiddheśva—itaśca parameśvara eva daharo 'sminnaṃtarākāśa ityucyate |*)**NOTE** यत्कारणमाकाशशब्दः परमेश्वरे प्रसिद्धः । (*yatkāraṇamākāśaśabdaḥ parameśvare prasiddhaḥ |*) आकाशो वै नाम.... ....स आत्मा सर्वाणि ह वा इमानि भूतान्याकाशादेव समुत्पद्यंते ( (*ākāśo vai nāma.... ....sa ātmā sarvāṇi ha vā imāni bhūtānyākāśādeva samutpadyaṃte (*) इत्यादि प्रयोगदर्शनात् ॥ (*ityādi prayogadarśanāt ‖*)
(Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya 1-3-17)

This inner heart-space is well known by the name Supreme Lord. Because space is the cause of the division of name and form, which are the outer manifestations of the Supreme Brahman, and because there are Śruti sentences such as "all these beings arise from space alone" which declare the identity of space with Brahman, the small space is well known in some places as the dwelling-place of Brahman and in others as of the very form of Brahman.

सा इयं शब्दब्रह्मात्मिका वाक् उत्कृष्टे हृदयाकाशे मूलाधारे सहस्राक्षरा अनेकाकारेण व्याप्ता भवति ॥ (*sā iyaṃ śabdabrahmātmikā vāk utkṛṣṭe hṛdayākāśe mūlādhāre sahasrākṣarā anekākāreṇa vyāptā bhavati ‖*)
(Śaṃ. Bhā.)**NOTE**

### Printed p. 608
This speech, of the form of the Word-Brahman, abiding in the Mūlādhāra, which is excellent and of the form of the heart-space, takes immeasurable shapes and pervades the universe. In such descriptions the identity of the Word-Brahman, called Gāyatrī, with the Brahman that is of the nature of space is stated. The Brahman described in this way is itself of the form of light. What the nature of this light called Brahman is, is described in the Upaniṣads as follows.

21. The light-form of the Supreme Principle.

अथ य एषोऽंतरे हृत्पुष्कर एवाश्रितोऽन्नमत्ति स एषोऽग्निर्दिवि श्रितः सौरः कालाख्योऽदृश्यः सर्वभूतान्यन्नमत्तीति । (*atha ya eṣo 'ṃtare hṛtpuṣkara evāśrito 'nnamatti sa eṣo 'gnirdivi śritaḥ sauraḥ kālākhyo 'dṛśyaḥ sarvabhūtānyannamattīti |*) कः पुष्करः किंमयो वेति। (*kaḥ puṣkaraḥ kiṃmayo veti|*) इदं नाव तत्पुष्करं योऽयमाकाशोऽस्यॆमाश्चतस्रो दिशश्चतस्र उपदिशो दलसंस्था आसं । (*idaṃ nāva tatpuṣkaraṃ yo 'yamākāśo 'syèmāścatasro diśaścatasra upadiśo dalasaṃsthā āsaṃ |*) अर्वाग्विचरत एतौ प्राणादित्या एता उपासीतोमित्येतदक्षरेण व्याहृतिभिः सावित्रा चेति ॥ (*arvāgvicarata etau prāṇādityā etā upāsītomityetadakṣareṇa vyāhṛtibhiḥ sāvitrā ceti ‖*)
(Maitrupaniṣat 6-2)**NOTE**

The Person who, abiding in the lotus of the heart, eats food, is the divine light, all-devouring, of the nature of Time, and of the form of the Sun. What is this lotus of the heart? What is its nature? The all-pervading space itself is this lotus of the heart. The four main directions and the four intermediate directions are the petals of this lotus of the form of space. The Self abiding in the lotus and the Sun abiding in space face each other. It is taught that this principle is to be contemplated by the Vyāhṛtis भूः (*bhūḥ*), भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*), स्वः (*svaḥ*), by the syllable Praṇava in the form of ओं (*oṃ*), and by the recitation of the Gāyatrī in the form of the Sāvitrī, तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यं भर्गॊ देवस्य धीमहि (*tatsaviturvareṇyaṃ bhargò devasya dhīmahi*).

The division भूः (*bhūḥ*), भुवः (*bhuvaḥ*), स्वः (*svaḥ*) describes the nature of Brahman, who is of the form of light, and equally the nature of the Praṇava and the Gāyatrī. It is said from the worldly point of view that Brahman is the end to be attained and the Praṇava and Gāyatrī are the means, and from the ordinary standpoint of the division into the object of worship and the means of worship. But the Śruti teaches that in the ultimate sense this end and means are to be understood as one. It must be chiefly noticed that the principle of the form of light can be known only by a means that is itself of the form of light. And this means is of the form of meditation. Therefore it must be examined, as is at present necessary: what is the light-nature of the Supreme Principle, the end; what is the light-nature of the Gāyatrī and the Praṇava, the means; what is the nature of the meditation that knows the Supreme Light; and, तत्त्ववितुः (*tattvavituḥ*)**NOTE**

### Printed p. 609
whether it can be said that in this one great mantra alone these three forms, end, means and meditation, are indicated.

स त्रेधात्मानं व्याकुरुतादित्यं तृतीयं वायुं तृतीयं स एष प्राणस्त्रेधा विहितः । (*sa tredhātmānaṃ vyākurutādityaṃ tṛtīyaṃ vāyuṃ tṛtīyaṃ sa eṣa prāṇastredhā vihitaḥ |*) तस्य प्राची दिक्किरोऽसौ चासौ चेर्मौ । (*tasya prācī dikkiro 'sau cāsau cermau |*) तस्य प्राची दिक्किरोऽसौ चेर्मौ । (*tasya prācī dikkiro 'sau cermau |*) आधास्य प्रतीची दिक्षुच्छमसौ चासौ च सक्थ्या दक्षिणा चोदीची च पार्श्वे द्यौः पृष्ठमंतरिक्षमुदरमियमुरः (*ādhāsya pratīcī dikṣucchamasau cāsau ca sakthyā dakṣiṇā codīcī ca pārśve dyauḥ pṛṣṭhamaṃtarikṣamudaramiyamuraḥ*) स एषोऽप्सु प्रतिष्ठितो यत्र क्व चैति तदेव प्रतितिष्ठत्येवं विद्वान् । (*sa eṣo 'psu pratiṣṭhito yatra kva caiti tadeva pratitiṣṭhatyevaṃ vidvān |*)
(Bṛ. U. 1-2-3)

This Supreme Brahman, described as the sacrificial horse, took three forms: one became known in the form of earthly fire, another in the form of the Sun, and the third in the form of the wind. It must be said that Prāṇa, whose nature is spiritual, itself has these three states. These three worlds, which contain the lights beginning with Agni, are like the limbs of the horse. The eastern quarter is its head, its forelegs and its flanks. The west is its hind feet and its two hind flanks. The bones on the two sides are the forms of south and north. The back is the heavenly world; the belly is the atmosphere; the chest is the earth. It is established in the waters. One who knows this principle is also firmly established. These three divisions were explained and stated before. In the special subjects of Ṛks such as त्रयः केशिनः ऋतुथा वि चक्षते (*trayaḥ keśinaḥ ṛtuthā vi cakṣate*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 164-44)**NOTE**, the three divisions of the Supreme Light described above are also described. The Supreme Light, which contains these three kinds of light or is itself of their form, is the Supreme Brahman. The golden Person within the Sun is that light itself, which in the Ṛksaṃhitā is described thus:

केश्यंग्निं केशी विषं केशी बिभर्ति रोदसी । केशी विश्वं स्वर्दृशे केशीदं ज्योतिरुच्यते ॥ (*keśyaṃgniṃ keśī viṣaṃ keśī bibharti rodasī | keśī viśvaṃ svardṛśe keśīdaṃ jyotirucyate ‖*)
(Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-136-1)

Keśin, that is, the Sun, radiant and of the nature of rays, bears fire and water. He bears heaven and earth. The whole universe beholds his form made of radiance. The lord of the universe, of such a light-form, has the name Keśin: thus it is described.

यज्योतिरमृतं ब्रह्म यद्योगात्समुपाश्नुते । तज्ज्ञानमभितुष्टाव सूक्तेनाथ बृहस्पतिः ॥ (*yajyotiramṛtaṃ brahma yadyogātsamupāśnute | tajjñānamabhituṣṭāva sūktenātha bṛhaspatiḥ ‖*)
(Bṛ. De. 7-109)

### Printed p. 610

Knowledge is the light that reveals the nature of Brahman. Only with its help is direct realisation of Brahman, whose form is light, possible. The Bṛhaddevatā states that Bṛhaspati (Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-71) praised that very light.

यत्र ज्योतिरजस्रं यस्मिल्लोके स्वर्हितं । तस्मिन् मां धेहि पवमानामृते लोके अक्षित इंद्रायेंदो परि स्रव ॥ (*yatra jyotirajasraṃ yasmilloke svarhitaṃ | tasmin māṃ dhehi pavamānāmṛte loke akṣita iṃdrāyeṃdo pari srava ‖*) (Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-113-7)

In Śruti passages such as this too there is a description of the nature of Brahman as light. The purport of the above passages is that this Brahman, whose form is light, shines in the three worlds, Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ and Svaḥ, in three forms: Agni, Vāyu and Āditya. These three lights are also indicated by other names:

अग्निर्वायुरादित्यः कालो यः प्राणोऽन्नं ब्रह्मारुद्रो मिष्णुरित्येकेऽन्य मभिध्यायंति ...॥ (*agnirvāyurādityaḥ kālo yaḥ prāṇo 'nnaṃ brahmārudro miṣṇurityeke 'nya mabhidhyāyaṃti ...‖*) (Maitrī Upaniṣad 4-5)**NOTE**

Some worship and indicate the three forms of this supreme light as Agni, Vāyu and Āditya; some as Kāla, Prāṇa and Anna; some as Brahmā, Rudra and Viṣṇu. If one asks which of these is the best and truly real, the praise in the Maitrī Upaniṣad is that the principle called Turīya, which is beyond all these embodied forms, is the Supreme Brahman. It was stated above that this is the fourth quarter of the Supreme Principle called Gāyatra. Describing these four quarters in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka, it praises thus: तस्या उपस्थानं गायत्रैकपदी, द्विपदी, त्रिपदी, चतुष्पद्यपदसि न हि पद्यसे । नमस्ते तुरीयाय दर्शताय पदाय परोरजसे (*tasyā upasthānaṃ gāyatraikapadī, dvipadī, tripadī, catuṣpadyapadasi na hi padyase | namaste turīyāya darśatāya padāya parorajase*) (Bṛ. U. 5-14-7). These four quarters, and the special meanings of epithets such as परोरजसे (*parorajase*), were explained above.

**22. The embodied forms of Brahman, whose form is the supreme light (the divisions of the Vyāhṛtis beginning with Bhūḥ)**

Just as it has been described how the Supreme Brahman, whose form is the supreme light, has evolved into the forms of light such as Agni, so it is stated in many places that the Praṇava, which consists of the Vyāhṛtis, has also evolved into the three worlds beginning with Bhūḥ, which are the support of the lights Agni, Vāyu and Āditya. And it is also settled that this Praṇava is none other than the Supreme Brahman. The Supreme Brahman, whose nature is Praṇava,

### Printed p. 611

evolving in three ways and being called by other names suited to each place and time and to its nature, and being praised as of the nature of the Supreme Brahman by the Gāyatrī called Sāvitrī, is clearly stated in the Maitrī Upaniṣad. From this it is also clearly understood that the Gāyatrī consisting of the Vyāhṛtis and the Praṇava consisting of the Vyāhṛtis are other names of one Brahman-principle whose form is light. उपासीत ओमित्येतदक्षरेण व्याहृतिभिः सावित्रा चेति (*upāsīta omityetadakṣareṇa vyāhṛtibhiḥ sāvitrā ceti*) (3-62-10): one should meditate with the Vyāhṛtis, with the Praṇava and with the recitation of the Sāvitrī, and so attain realisation of Brahman. That Brahman-principle which is thus praised is described as having evolved in the form of the Vyāhṛtis and in the form of the Praṇava,**NOTE**, and is praised by the Gāyatrī.

द्वे नाव ब्रह्मणो रूपे मूर्तं चामूर्तं चाथ तदसत्यं यदमूर्तं तत्सत्यं तद्ब्रह्म तज्योतिः यज्योतिः स आदित्यः स वा एष ओमित्येतदात्माभवत् स त्रेधात्मानं व्यकुरुता ओमिति तिस्रो मात्रा एताभिः सर्वमिदमोतं प्रोतं चैवास्मीत्येवं ह्याहैतद्वा आदित्य ओमित्येवं ध्यायत आत्मानं युंजीतेति ॥ (*dve nāva brahmaṇo rūpe mūrtaṃ cāmūrtaṃ cātha tadasatyaṃ yadamūrtaṃ tatsatyaṃ tadbrahma tajyotiḥ yajyotiḥ sa ādityaḥ sa vā eṣa omityetadātmābhavat sa tredhātmānaṃ vyakurutā omiti tisro mātrā etābhiḥ sarvamidamotaṃ protaṃ caivāsmītyevaṃ hyāhaitadvā āditya omityevaṃ dhyāyata ātmānaṃ yuṃjīteti ‖*) (Mai. U. 6-3)**NOTE**

Brahman has two forms: embodied and unembodied. The embodied is unreal; the unembodied is real. That is Brahman, real and of the form of light. This light is Āditya. For this Brahman, who is of the form of light and of the nature of Āditya, the Praṇava, the syllable Oṃ, is the Self. (As it is said in the Bṛhadāraṇyaka that Brahman evolved into three forms, Agni, Āditya and Vāyu, here too the same kind of division is stated.) This Praṇava has three forms: the letter a, the letter u and the letter m. By these parts of the Praṇava, a, u and m, the whole world is woven together like warp and woof (ota and prota). For that very reason Āditya, who is the Self of the universe, should be worshipped as of the nature of the Praṇava.

In the embodied form the nature of this Praṇava is threefold. These portions may also be called the limbs of the Supreme Self. Their forms are as follows:

अथान्यत्राप्युक्तं स्वनवत्येषास्य तनूर्या ओमिति (*athānyatrāpyuktaṃ svanavatyeṣāsya tanūryā omiti*) (Ā. U. Ma.)**NOTE**

अथ स्त्री, पुं, नपुंसक इति .... .... लिंगवत्येषा (*atha strī, puṃ, napuṃsaka iti .... .... liṃgavatyeṣā*)

अथ अग्निः, वायुः, आदित्य इति .... .... भास्वत्येषा (*atha agniḥ, vāyuḥ, āditya iti .... .... bhāsvatyeṣā*)

अथ ब्रह्म, रुद्रो. विष्णुरिति .... .... अधिपतिवत्येषा (*atha brahma, rudro. viṣṇuriti .... .... adhipativatyeṣā*)

अथ गार्हपत्यो दक्षिणाग्निराहवनीय इति .... मुखवत्येषा (*atha gārhapatyo dakṣiṇāgnirāhavanīya iti .... mukhavatyeṣā*)

अथ ऋग्यजुः सामेति .... .... विज्ञानवत्येषा (*atha ṛgyajuḥ sāmeti .... .... vijñānavatyeṣā*)

### Printed p. 612

अथ भूः, भुवः, स्वः इति (*atha bhūḥ, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ iti*) …. …. लोकवत्येषा (*lokavatyeṣā*)

अथ भूतं भव्यं भविष्यदिति (*atha bhūtaṃ bhavyaṃ bhaviṣyaditi*) …. …. कालवत्येषा (*kālavatyeṣā*)

अथ प्राणोऽग्निस्ूर्य इति (*atha prāṇo 'gnisūrya iti*) …. …. प्रतापवत्येषा (*pratāpavatyeṣā*)

अथ अन्नमापश्चंद्रमा इति (*atha annamāpaścaṃdramā iti*) …. …. आप्यायनवत्येषा (*āpyāyanavatyeṣā*)

अथ बुद्धिर्मनोऽहंकार इति (*atha buddhirmano 'haṃkāra iti*) …. …. चेतनवत्येषा (*cetanavatyeṣā*)

अथ प्राणोऽपानो व्यान इति (*atha prāṇo 'pāno vyāna iti*) …. …. प्राणवत्येषा (*prāṇavatyeṣā*)

इत्यत ओमित्युक्तेनैताः प्रस्तुता अर्चिता अर्पिता भंवतीत्येवं .... .... .... ब्रह्मयदोमित्येतदक्षरमिति । (*ityata omityuktenaitāḥ prastutā arcitā arpitā bhaṃvatītyevaṃ .... .... .... brahmayadomityetadakṣaramiti |*) (Maitrī Upaniṣad 6-2)**NOTE**

Female, male and neuter: this is the division by gender. Agni, Vāyu and Āditya: this is of the nature of light. Brahmā, Rudra and Viṣṇu: this is in the form of lordship. Gārhapatya, Dakṣiṇāgni and Āhavanīya: this is of the nature of the mouth. Ṛk, Yajus and Sāman: this is of the nature of knowledge. It is of the nature of the worlds as Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ and Svaḥ; of the nature of time as past, present and future; of the form of heat as Prāṇa, Agni and Sūrya; of the form of growth as Anna, Āpaḥ and Candramas; of the form of consciousness as Buddhi, Manas and Ahaṃkāra; and of the form of life-breath as Prāṇa, Apāna and Vyāna. For this very reason Brahman is to be worshipped in the form of the Praṇava. The whole world also has the nature of the Vyāhṛtis, which are the parts of the Praṇava. For this very reason this Brahman is to be worshipped by the mantra तत्सवितुः (*tatsavituḥ*), which is a prayer addressed to the deity Savitṛ.

**23. The Vyāhṛtis, which are the forms of the world beginning with the earth, are the chief means of worshipping Brahman, the root of it**

In the above explanation, and also in the section that follows, two points should be noted. First, that the three worlds beginning with the earth were produced by the utterance of the Vyāhṛtis beginning with Bhūḥ. Second, that for this very reason Brahman is to be worshipped by means of the Vyāhṛtis, which are of the nature of the Gāyatrī.

अथाव्याहृतं वा इदमासीत् स सत्यं प्रजापतिस्तपस्तप्त्वा नुव्याहरदर्भुवस्स्वरित्येष्टैवास्य प्रजापतेः स्थविष्ठा तनूर्या लोकवतीति स्वरित्यस्याः शिरो नाभिर्भुवो भूः पादा आदित्यश्चक्षुः । चक्षुरायत्ता हि पुरुषस्य महती मात्रा चक्षुषा ह्ययं मात्राश्चरति सत्यं वै चक्षुरक्षिण्यवस्थितो हि पुरुष (*athāvyāhṛtaṃ vā idamāsīt sa satyaṃ prajāpatistapastaptvā nuvyāharadarbhuvassvarityeṣṭaivāsya prajāpateḥ sthaviṣṭhā tanūryā lokavatīti svarityasyāḥ śiro nābhirbhuvo bhūḥ pādā ādityaścakṣuḥ | cakṣurāyattā hi puruṣasya mahatī mātrā cakṣuṣā hyayaṃ mātrāścarati satyaṃ vai cakṣurakṣiṇyavasthito hi puruṣa*)

### Printed p. 613

सर्वार्थेषु चरत्येतस्मात् भूर्भुवः स्वरित्युपासीतानेन हि प्रजापतिर्विश्वात्मा विश्वचक्षुरिवोपासितो भवतीत्येवं ह्याहैषा वै .... .... तस्मादेषोपासीत ॥ (*sarvārtheṣu caratyetasmāt bhūrbhuvaḥ svarityupāsītānena hi prajāpatirviśvātmā viśvacakṣurivopāsito bhavatītyevaṃ hyāhaiṣā vai .... .... tasmādeṣopāsīta ‖*) (Mai. U. 6-6)

In the beginning this universe was unmanifest. The Supreme Person, real in nature and in the form of Prajāpati, performed austerity and uttered: Bhūḥ (the earth), Bhuvaḥ (the atmosphere), Svaḥ (the world of Āditya). This is the gross form of Prajāpati, consisting of the universe. The world of Āditya is the head of this form; the atmosphere is the navel; the earth is the feet. The eye, the means of seeing everything, is of the form of Āditya. For this very reason Brahman is to be worshipped by the means consisting of the Vyāhṛtis Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ. Brahman, in the form of Prajāpati, is the inner self of all worlds, the divine eye, and the one worshipped by the whole world. The Brahman in whom the whole universe is contained, in the form of Prajāpati, is to be worshipped by the Gāyatrī mantra, which is called Sāvitrī and is of the form of the Vyāhṛtis. Its method is as follows:

तत्सवितुर्वरेण्यमित्यसौ ना आदित्यः सविता स वा एवं प्रवरणीय आत्मकामेनेत्याहुर्ब्रह्मवादिनः ॥ (*tatsaviturvareṇyamityasau nā ādityaḥ savitā sa vā evaṃ pravaraṇīya ātmakāmenetyāhurbrahmavādinaḥ ‖*)

"That most worshipful great radiance of Savitṛ": who is that Savitṛ? Āditya, who shines in the heavenly world, is Savitṛ. The Brahmavādins have taught that a person who desires to contemplate the Self should worship this Savitṛ, knowing his nature.

भर्गो देवस्य धीमहीति सविता वै देवस्ततो योऽस्य भर्गाख्यस्तं चिंतयामीत्याहुर्ब्रह्मवादिनः ॥ (*bhargo devasya dhīmahīti savitā vai devastato yo 'sya bhargākhyastaṃ ciṃtayāmītyāhurbrahmavādinaḥ ‖*)

"May we know and meditate on the Bharga of that Savitṛ." This Savitṛ is the Supreme Brahman. The teaching of the Brahmavādins is that one should contemplate him.

धियो यो नः प्रचोदयात् इति बुद्धयो वै धियः यो नः प्रचोदयादिति बुद्धयो वै धियस्ता योऽस्माकं प्रचोदयादित्याहुर्ब्रह्मावादिनः ॥ (*dhiyo yo naḥ pracodayāt iti buddhayo vai dhiyaḥ yo naḥ pracodayāditi buddhayo vai dhiyastā yo 'smākaṃ pracodayādityāhurbrahmāvādinaḥ ‖*) (Mai. U. 6-7)

"May that same Savitṛ produce insight in us; may he give us the vitality to know the Bharga of Savitṛ": this is what one should pray, the Brahmavādins have said. Thus the Maitrī Upaniṣad gives an explanation in the form of a derivation of the Ṛk beginning तत्सवितुः (*tatsavituḥ*). It will be stated later among the special topics of this same mantra.

### Printed p. 614

**24. Direct realisation of this light, famed as the Bharga of Savitṛ, is possible only through meditation.**

अथ यदतः पुरो दिवो ज्योतिर्दिप्यते विश्वतः पृष्ठेषु सर्वतः पृष्ठेष्वनुत्तमेषूत्तमेषु लोकेष्टिदं वाव तद्यदिदमस्मिन्नंतः पुरुषे ज्योतिः ॥ ( (*atha yadataḥ puro divo jyotirdipyate viśvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣu sarvataḥ pṛṣṭheṣvanuttameṣūttameṣu lokeṣṭidaṃ vāva tadyadidamasminnaṃtaḥ puruṣe jyotiḥ ‖ (*) (Chā. U. 3-13-7)

The great light that shines in the highest world, beyond the heavenly world and beyond which there is no other world, is the very light that shines also in the lotus of the heart of man. The great radiance so described in the Chāndogya and other texts is praised here under the name of the Bharga of Savitṛ. This light is the supreme light of the Supreme Principle. For this reason it is indicated in the Brahmasūtra by the sūtra ज्योतिश्चरणाभिधानात् (*jyotiścaraṇābhidhānāt*) (Bra. Sū. 1-1-25). The objection that may be raised on this occasion, put by the opponent, and the answer given to it, were also stated above.
